questions.question: Why water molecules are called amphoteric in nature?
questions.answer: Water is called amphoteric (amphiprotic) because it can act both as an acid and as a base. It donates a proton to a base (forming OH⁻) and accepts a proton from an acid (forming H₃O⁺). Pure water also ionizes slightly: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
questions.explanation: Amphoteric substances can both donate and accept protons; water's ability makes it an excellent solvent and buffer in living systems.

questions.question: Why amino acids are named so?
questions.answer: They are named amino acids because each molecule contains an amino group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH), both attached to the same asymmetric α-carbon atom.
questions.explanation: The name combines 'amino' and 'carboxylic acid', the two functional groups that define this class of molecules.

questions.question: How monosaccharides are classified?
questions.answer: Monosaccharides are classified by the number of carbon atoms: trioses (3C), tetroses (4C), pentoses (5C), hexoses (6C) and heptoses (7C). They are also classified by the carbonyl group as aldoses (aldehyde group) and ketoses (ketone group).
questions.explanation: Examples: glyceraldehyde (triose), ribose (pentose), glucose (hexose); glucose is an aldose while fructose is a ketose.

questions.question: Enlist bio-elements make 98 % of living system?
questions.answer: Carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O) and nitrogen (N) together make about 98% of the living system. The remaining 2% includes phosphorus, sulphur, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sodium, chlorine and iron.
questions.explanation: C, H, O and N are the major bio-elements because they form the backbones of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

questions.question: Why fats provide more energy than carbohydrates?
questions.answer: Fats provide more energy because their fatty acid chains are more reduced — they contain more C–H bonds and less oxygen per carbon than carbohydrates. Oxidation of fat therefore releases about 9 kcal/g, compared with about 4 kcal/g for carbohydrates.
questions.explanation: Energy yield depends on the degree of reduction; fat is also stored anhydrously, making it a compact energy store.

questions.question: How many steps involve in nucleotide formation?
questions.answer: Nucleotide formation involves three steps: (1) formation of the pentose sugar (ribose or deoxyribose); (2) attachment of a nitrogenous base to the sugar to form a nucleoside; (3) attachment of one or more phosphate groups to the nucleoside to form a nucleotide.
questions.explanation: Nucleoside = sugar + base; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.

questions.question: Distinguish between saturated acylglycerol and unsaturated acylglycerols.
questions.answer: Saturated acylglycerols contain only saturated fatty acids (no C=C double bonds); their chains are straight, they pack tightly, have a higher melting point and are usually solid at room temperature (e.g. animal fats). Unsaturated acylglycerols contain one or more C=C double bonds; the kinked chains pack loosely, giving a lower melting point and a liquid state at room temperature (e.g. vegetable oils).
questions.explanation: Double bonds prevent close packing, so unsaturated fats/oils melt at lower temperatures.

questions.question: Describe the properties and roles of starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin.
questions.answer:
Starch: homopolymer of α-glucose with amylose (unbranched, α-1,4) and amylopectin (branched, α-1,6); main energy-storage carbohydrate of plants (seeds, tubers); gives blue-black colour with iodine; digested by amylase.

Glycogen: highly branched polymer of α-glucose; the animal storage carbohydrate ('animal starch'), stored in liver and muscle cells; its many branch ends allow rapid glucose release.

Cellulose: unbranched polymer of β-glucose joined by β-1,4 linkages; straight chains form microfibrils; structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls and the most abundant carbohydrate in nature; humans cannot digest it (no cellulase) but it provides dietary fibre; ruminants digest it with microbial help.

Chitin: polymer of N-acetylglucosamine with β-1,4 linkages; forms the exoskeleton of arthropods and the cell walls of fungi; tough, waterproof and resistant; second most abundant polysaccharide after cellulose.
questions.explanation: All four are glucose/amino-sugar polymers, but their linkage type and branching determine whether they serve storage (starch, glycogen) or structure (cellulose, chitin).

questions.question: What is nucleic acid? Describe structure of a mononucleotide (ATP) and a dinucleotide (NAD).
questions.answer:
Nucleic acids are biopolymers of nucleotides that store and transmit genetic information; DNA is double-stranded and RNA is single-stranded.

Mononucleotide (ATP): ATP is adenosine triphosphate — adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups. The base is joined to ribose (nucleoside adenosine), and three phosphates are attached to the 5′ carbon. Hydrolysis of the terminal phosphate releases about 7.3 kcal/mol, so ATP is the universal energy carrier.

Dinucleotide (NAD): nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide consists of two nucleotides joined by a phosphodiester bond — adenine-ribose-phosphate–phosphate-ribose-nicotinamide. NAD is a coenzyme that carries electrons and hydrogen in redox reactions of respiration and fermentation.
questions.explanation: A nucleotide has three parts (sugar, base, phosphate); adding a second nucleotide through a phosphodiester bond gives a dinucleotide.

questions.question: What is amino acid? Explain peptide linkage formation.
questions.answer:
An amino acid is an organic compound containing an amino group (–NH₂) and a carboxyl group (–COOH) attached to the same asymmetric α-carbon, along with a hydrogen atom and a variable R (side-chain) group. About 20 standard amino acids occur in proteins; the R group determines their properties.

Peptide linkage: when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is removed (condensation) and a –CO–NH– bond called a peptide bond is formed. Repeating this process links many amino acids into a polypeptide chain, which folds into a protein. The reaction is catalysed by the ribosome during protein synthesis.
questions.explanation: The peptide bond is a covalent amide linkage; the repeating N–C–C backbone plus R groups gives each protein its unique sequence and shape.

questions.question: Explain classification of protein and list structural and functional protein.
questions.answer:
Proteins are classified in three ways:
1. By structure: fibrous proteins (long, insoluble, structural — keratin, collagen, myosin) and globular proteins (rounded, soluble, functional — albumin, haemoglobin, enzymes).
2. By composition: simple proteins (only amino acids — albumin, globulin) and conjugated proteins (protein + non-protein prosthetic group — glycoproteins, lipoproteins, nucleoproteins, metalloproteins).
3. By function: structural (collagen, keratin), catalytic (enzymes), transport (haemoglobin, membrane carriers), hormonal/regulatory (insulin, growth hormone), defensive (immunoglobulins), contractile (actin, myosin), storage (casein, ovalbumin) and receptor proteins.

Structural proteins: keratin (hair, nails), collagen (skin, tendons, bone), actin and myosin (muscle).
Functional proteins: enzymes (amylase, catalase), haemoglobin (oxygen transport), insulin (hormone), antibodies (defence).
questions.explanation: Fibrous proteins are insoluble and structural; globular proteins are soluble and functional. Conjugated proteins carry a non-protein prosthetic group.

questions.question: What are lipids? Explain acylglycerol and waxes.
questions.answer:
Lipids are a diverse group of hydrophobic organic compounds that are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents (ether, chloroform). They include fats and oils, phospholipids, waxes, terpenoids, steroids and prostaglandins, and serve in energy storage, membranes, insulation, protection and hormone action.

Acylglycerols (glycerides): esters of glycerol with one, two or three fatty acids. Monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides are formed by ester bonds between the –OH groups of glycerol and the –COOH groups of fatty acids. Triglycerides are the main storage lipids; fats are solid and oils liquid at room temperature.

Waxes: esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain alcohols. They are highly hydrophobic and form protective waterproof coatings on leaves, stems, fruits, feathers and the insect cuticle, reducing water loss and preventing microbial attack.
questions.explanation: Both are esters of long-chain fatty acids; acylglycerols are storage lipids while waxes are protective structural lipids.

questions.question: Explain terpenoids and its types.
questions.answer:
Terpenoids (isoprenoids) are lipids built from repeating five-carbon isoprene (C₅H₈) units. They are synthesized from acetyl-CoA through the mevalonate pathway and include many pigments, essential oils, vitamins and hormones.

Types by number of isoprene units:
1. Monoterpenes (C₁₀, 2 units): essential oils such as menthol, camphor and limonene.
2. Sesquiterpenes (C₁₅, 3 units): farnesol and some plant defensive compounds.
3. Diterpenes (C₂₀, 4 units): gibberellins and tocopherols (vitamin E).
4. Triterpenes (C₃₀, 6 units): squalene and steroids.
5. Tetraterpenes (C₄₀, 8 units): carotenoids such as carotene and xanthophyll (photosynthetic pigments).
6. Polyterpenes: natural rubber (many isoprene units).
questions.explanation: Terpenoids are classified by the number of C₅ isoprene units they contain; the classes differ in volatility and function.

questions.question: What are conjugated molecules? Explain types of conjugated molecules.
questions.answer:
Conjugated molecules are formed when biomolecules belonging to two different groups combine chemically and act as a single functional unit. The non-protein part is called the prosthetic group.

Types:
1. Glycoproteins: carbohydrate + protein (mucin, antibodies, cell-surface receptors).
2. Lipoproteins: lipid + protein (HDL, LDL, VLDL) — transport lipids in blood.
3. Nucleoproteins: nucleic acid + protein (chromatin = DNA + histones; ribosomes = rRNA + proteins).
4. Metalloproteins: metal ion + protein (haemoglobin = Fe, chlorophyll protein = Mg, carbonic anhydrase = Zn).
5. Chromoproteins: coloured pigment + protein (haemoglobin, chlorophyll).
6. Phosphoproteins: phosphate group + protein (casein of milk).
questions.explanation: Conjugation attaches a non-protein prosthetic group to a protein, giving the molecule new properties such as colour, electron transfer or lipid solubility.

questions.question: Why enzymes are specific in nature?
questions.answer: Enzymes are specific because each enzyme has an active site with a particular shape, charge and chemical environment that is complementary only to its own substrate. Only that substrate can bind and form the enzyme–substrate complex, so each enzyme catalyses one type of reaction.
questions.explanation: Specificity results from the precise folding of the protein chain around the active site (lock-and-key or induced fit).

questions.question: Why enzyme activity is directly proportional to enzyme concentration?
questions.answer: When substrate is present in excess, each enzyme molecule provides active sites for catalysis. Increasing the enzyme concentration increases the number of active sites, so more substrate molecules are converted per unit time; the rate therefore rises in direct proportion to enzyme concentration.
questions.explanation: The proportionality holds only while substrate is not limiting; at very high substrate the rate becomes independent of further enzyme increase only if substrate is exhausted.

questions.question: Why enzymes are called temperature sensitive?
questions.answer: Enzyme activity rises with temperature up to an optimum (about 37 °C in humans) because molecular collisions increase. Above the optimum, heat breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds holding the protein's tertiary structure, the active site loses its shape and the enzyme is denatured; activity then falls sharply. At low temperatures the enzyme is inactive but not denatured.
questions.explanation: Denaturation is irreversible in most cases; this is why high fever or boiling destroys enzyme function.

questions.question: How enzyme reduces the energy of activation?
questions.answer: The enzyme binds the substrate at its active site and brings reacting molecules close together in the correct orientation. It strains or distorts the substrate's bonds, stabilizes the transition state and provides a favourable microenvironment (e.g. acidic or non-polar). These effects lower the activation energy, so the reaction occurs rapidly at body temperature.
questions.explanation: The enzyme is not consumed; after product release it returns to its original form and can catalyse again.

questions.question: How enzymes activity effect on substrate concentration?
questions.answer: At low substrate concentration the rate increases almost linearly with substrate concentration because more substrate molecules collide with active sites. As concentration rises, more active sites become occupied until all are saturated; the rate then levels off at a maximum (Vmax) and further substrate has little effect.
questions.explanation: This saturation kinetics is described by the Michaelis–Menten curve; Km is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax.

questions.question: What do you mean by prosthetic group?
questions.answer: A prosthetic group is a non-protein component (organic molecule or metal ion) that is tightly and permanently bound to a conjugated enzyme and is essential for its catalytic activity. Examples are the haem group of catalase and peroxidase, FAD of flavoproteins and biotin of carboxylases.
questions.explanation: Prosthetic groups are a type of cofactor; coenzymes are loosely attached cofactors such as NAD and coenzyme A.

questions.question: Differentiate between the activator and inhibitors.
questions.answer: Activators are substances that increase enzyme activity by binding to the enzyme and stabilizing its active conformation (e.g. Cl⁻ for salivary amylase, Mg²⁺ for kinases). Inhibitors are substances that decrease or stop enzyme activity: competitive inhibitors bind the active site, noncompetitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and change enzyme shape, and uncompetitive inhibitors bind the enzyme–substrate complex.
questions.explanation: Activators promote catalysis; inhibitors block it and are important in metabolic regulation and drug action.

questions.question: What is enzyme? explain characteristics of enzyme.
questions.answer:
An enzyme is a biological catalyst, almost always a globular protein (a few are RNA ribozymes), that accelerates a specific chemical reaction by lowering its activation energy without being consumed.

Characteristics:
1. High catalytic efficiency — increases reaction rate by 10⁶–10¹³ times.
2. Specificity — each enzyme acts on a particular substrate or type of bond.
3. Reversible action — catalyses the reaction in either direction.
4. Temperature sensitive — maximum activity at an optimum temperature; denatured by heat.
5. pH sensitive — each enzyme has an optimum pH (e.g. pepsin ≈ 2, trypsin ≈ 8).
6. Required in small amounts and not consumed in the reaction.
7. Many need cofactors (coenzymes, prosthetic groups or metal ions).
8. Act in aqueous medium and are often compartmentalized within cells.
9. Can be inhibited or activated by specific substances.
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy, so reactions proceed rapidly under mild cellular conditions.

questions.question: Describe the effect if temperature on the rate of enzyme action.
questions.answer:
Temperature strongly affects enzyme activity:
1. At low temperature, molecules have little kinetic energy, so collisions between enzyme and substrate are infrequent and activity is low (but the enzyme is not destroyed).
2. As temperature rises, activity increases; the rate roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise (Q₁₀ effect) because more enzyme–substrate complexes form.
3. At the optimum temperature (about 37 °C for human enzymes) activity is maximum.
4. Above the optimum, thermal energy breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds in the protein, the tertiary structure unfolds and the active site loses its shape — the enzyme is denatured. Activity falls rapidly and cannot be restored by cooling.
5. Enzymes from thermophilic organisms (e.g. hot-spring bacteria) have high optimum temperatures.

Practical importance: refrigeration slows enzyme action and preserves food, while cooking, sterilization and high fever denature enzymes.
questions.explanation: The curve of rate versus temperature is bell-shaped, with a sharp drop after the optimum due to denaturation.

questions.question: Describe mechanism of enzyme action.
questions.answer:
Enzyme action involves formation of an enzyme–substrate (ES) complex at the active site:
1. The substrate binds to the binding site of the active site.
2. The catalytic site converts the substrate into the transition state, straining its bonds and stabilizing the unstable intermediate.
3. The reaction proceeds with a much lower activation energy.
4. Products are released and the enzyme returns unchanged, ready to catalyse again.

Two models explain substrate binding:
- Lock-and-key model (Fischer): the active site is rigid and has a shape exactly complementary to the substrate.
- Induced fit model (Koshland): the active site is flexible; substrate binding induces a conformational change that tightens the fit and brings catalytic groups into position.

Factors such as temperature, pH, substrate and enzyme concentration, inhibitors and cofactors influence the rate of this cycle.
questions.explanation: Both models agree that catalysis depends on a precise, complementary active site; induced fit better explains specificity and strain.

questions.question: Describe the classification of enzymes.
questions.answer:
Enzymes are classified in several ways:

A. By the type of reaction catalysed (International classification):
1. Oxidoreductases — oxidation–reduction (dehydrogenases, oxidases, catalase).
2. Transferases — transfer of a group (kinases, transaminases).
3. Hydrolases — hydrolysis of bonds (amylase, lipase, protease).
4. Lyases — removal of groups without water (decarboxylases).
5. Isomerases — rearrangement of atoms (phosphoglucose isomerase).
6. Ligases (synthetases) — join molecules with ATP (DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase).

B. By substrate: proteases (proteins), lipases (fats), glycosidases (carbohydrates — amylase, maltase, sucrase, lactase, cellulase) and nucleases (nucleic acids).

C. By location: endoenzymes (act inside the cell) and exoenzymes (secreted outside, e.g. digestive enzymes).

D. By composition: simple enzymes (protein only) and conjugated enzymes (protein + cofactor/prosthetic group).
questions.explanation: The reaction-based classification is the most systematic; substrate names are often used in digestion and clinical contexts.

questions.question: Describe enzymatic inhibition, its types and its significance.
questions.answer:
Enzyme inhibition is the decrease or loss of enzyme activity by a substance called an inhibitor. It may be irreversible (inhibitor permanently modifies the enzyme) or reversible.

Types of reversible inhibition:
1. Competitive inhibition: the inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds to the active site, blocking entry of the substrate. It can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration (e.g. malonate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase).
2. Noncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds at an allosteric site, changing the shape of the enzyme/active site; increasing substrate cannot overcome it (e.g. cyanide on cytochrome oxidase).
3. Uncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex.

Significance:
- Regulation of metabolic pathways (feedback inhibition by end products).
- Protection against excess metabolites.
- Basis of drug action: penicillin inhibits bacterial transpeptidase; statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase.
- Poisons and toxins act as enzyme inhibitors.
- Used experimentally to study reaction mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site; noncompetitive inhibitors distort the enzyme from a separate site.

questions.question: Describe structure of enzyme.
questions.answer:
Enzymes are globular proteins whose function depends on their three-dimensional shape:
1. Primary structure — the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
2. Secondary structure — α-helices and β-pleated sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds.
3. Tertiary structure — folding of the chain into a compact globular shape stabilized by hydrogen, ionic, hydrophobic and disulphide bonds. Some enzymes also have quaternary structure (two or more polypeptide chains).

Within this folded structure is the active site — a small pocket or cleft formed by amino acid R groups brought together by folding. It has two parts: a binding site that holds the substrate and a catalytic site that brings about the reaction. The active site is complementary in shape and charge to the substrate.

Conjugated enzymes also contain a tightly bound prosthetic group or loosely bound coenzyme (e.g. haem, FAD, NAD) that assists catalysis. Allosteric sites elsewhere on the molecule allow regulation by activators or inhibitors.
questions.explanation: Denaturation destroys the tertiary structure and therefore the active site, permanently abolishing activity.

questions.question: Explain the effect of substrate and concentration on the rate of enzyme action.
questions.answer:
Effect of substrate concentration: at low substrate concentration the rate of reaction is directly proportional to substrate concentration, because more substrate molecules collide with active sites. As the concentration increases, more and more active sites become occupied; when all active sites are saturated the rate reaches a maximum (Vmax) and further increase in substrate produces no further increase in rate. The substrate concentration at which half of Vmax is reached is the Michaelis constant (Km), a measure of the enzyme's affinity for its substrate (low Km = high affinity).

Effect of enzyme concentration: when substrate is in excess, the rate is directly proportional to enzyme concentration, since more enzyme molecules provide more active sites. If substrate is limiting, adding more enzyme has little effect because substrate molecules are already being converted as fast as possible.

Both effects are used in clinical assays and industrial processes to optimize reaction conditions.
questions.explanation: The saturation curve is hyperbolic; Vmax reflects the turnover capacity and Km reflects substrate affinity.

questions.question: Why lysosome is called suicidal sacs?
questions.answer: Lysosomes contain powerful hydrolytic enzymes. If their membrane ruptures, these enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell's own components, causing autolysis and cell death. Because they can destroy the cell that contains them, lysosomes are called suicidal sacs.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions the membrane keeps the enzymes contained; release occurs during programmed cell death or injury.

questions.question: Why plasma membrane is differentially permeable in nature?
questions.answer: The phospholipid bilayer allows small non-polar molecules and water to pass, but restricts ions and large polar molecules. Membrane proteins provide channels and carriers for specific substances. Because it permits some substances to pass and not others, the plasma membrane is differentially (selectively) permeable.
questions.explanation: This selectivity maintains a distinct internal environment and is the basis of osmosis and active transport.

questions.question: Why plant cell wall is rigid?
questions.answer: The plant cell wall is rigid because it is made of cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin, and secondary walls are strengthened by lignin. These fibres resist stretching and give tensile strength. The wall is further stiffened by turgor pressure of the cell contents.
questions.explanation: Rigidity provides support and protection while allowing water and solutes to pass through the porous wall.

questions.question: Why chloroplast is called energy converting cell organelle?
questions.answer: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and the photosystems that absorb light energy. In photosynthesis they convert light energy into chemical energy (ATP and NADPH), which is then used to fix CO₂ into carbohydrates. Because they transform one form of energy into another, chloroplasts are called energy-converting organelles.
questions.explanation: Light energy → chemical energy → sugar; oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.question: How prokaryotic ribosome is different from eukaryotic ribosome.
questions.answer: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits, and are smaller with fewer proteins and RNA molecules. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, made of 60S and 40S subunits, and are larger. Prokaryotic (70S) ribosomes are the target of several antibiotics, whereas eukaryotic 80S ribosomes are not affected by them.
questions.explanation: S = Svedberg unit (sedimentation coefficient), a measure of size/density.

questions.question: How mitochondria is similar to bacteria?
questions.answer: Mitochondria resemble bacteria in having a double membrane, their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and the ability to divide by binary fission. Their size is also bacterium-like. These similarities support the endosymbiotic theory that mitochondria arose from engulfed aerobic bacteria.
questions.explanation: Because they contain their own genome and ribosomes, mitochondria are called semi-autonomous organelles.

questions.question: Why mitochondria is called power house of cell?
questions.answer: Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration. They oxidize pyruvate and fatty acids and carry out oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane, producing most of the cell's ATP. Since ATP is the energy currency that powers cellular activities, mitochondria are called the power house of the cell.
questions.explanation: Muscle, liver and active cells contain large numbers of mitochondria.

questions.question: Differentiate between peroxisome and glyoxysome.
questions.answer:
Peroxisome: a single-membrane organelle containing catalase and oxidases. It detoxifies hydrogen peroxide and alcohol, carries out β-oxidation of fatty acids and participates in photorespiration in leaves.

Glyoxysome: a specialized peroxisome found in the fat-storing storage tissues of germinating seeds. It contains enzymes of the glyoxylate cycle, which convert stored fats into carbohydrates (sugars) to support early seedling growth.
questions.explanation: Both are microbodies, but glyoxysomes have the additional glyoxylate-cycle enzymes needed to convert fat into sugar.

questions.question: Describe structure and functions of rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.answer:
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranes extending through the cytoplasm, continuous with the nuclear envelope.

Rough ER: bears ribosomes on its outer surface and consists of flattened, stacked cisternae. It synthesizes secretory and membrane proteins, folds them, adds carbohydrate chains (glycosylation) and transports them to the Golgi apparatus. It is abundant in protein-secreting cells such as pancreatic and liver cells.

Smooth ER: lacks ribosomes and is more tubular. It synthesizes lipids, phospholipids and steroid hormones, detoxifies drugs and alcohol (especially in liver cells), stores calcium ions (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle) and helps in glycogen metabolism.

Functions summarized: protein synthesis and processing (rough ER), lipid/steroid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage (smooth ER), and intracellular transport of materials.
questions.explanation: The two ER types are continuous but have different distributions and functions depending on the cell type.

questions.question: Explain the chemical composition and functions of plasma membrane in regulating cell's interactions with environment.
questions.answer:
Chemical composition: the plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer (about 40–50% lipid) with proteins (about 50%), cholesterol, glycolipids and glycoproteins. Phospholipids are arranged with hydrophilic heads outward and hydrophobic tails inward; proteins are either embedded (integral) or attached at the surface (peripheral). The fluid mosaic model describes proteins drifting in the lipid bilayer.

Functions:
1. Selective permeability — controls entry and exit of water, ions, nutrients and wastes by diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport.
2. Protection — forms a boundary between the cytoplasm and the environment.
3. Receptors — membrane proteins receive hormones and other chemical signals and trigger responses.
4. Cell recognition — glycoproteins and glycolipids act as identity markers.
5. Cell adhesion and junctions with neighbouring cells.
6. Enzyme activity — many membrane proteins are enzymes.
7. Endocytosis and exocytosis — bulk transport of materials.
8. Maintains the electrochemical gradient and cell shape.
questions.explanation: The membrane's protein and lipid composition varies between cell types according to their functions.

questions.question: Explain the structure and functions of lysosomes.
questions.answer:
Structure: lysosomes are small, spherical, single-membrane vesicles (0.1–1.2 µm) formed by budding from the Golgi apparatus. They contain about 40 hydrolytic enzymes — proteases, lipases, nucleases, glycosidases, phosphatases and sulphatases — that work best at acidic pH (about 5) maintained by proton pumps in the membrane.

Functions:
1. Intracellular digestion of materials taken in by endocytosis (heterophagy) — e.g. bacteria engulfed by white blood cells.
2. Autophagy — digestion of worn-out organelles and cell components.
3. Autolysis — release of enzymes to digest the whole cell after death or injury ('suicidal sacs').
4. Extracellular digestion — release of enzymes outside the cell (e.g. osteoclasts digesting bone).
5. Digestion of food particles in protozoa and macrophages.

Defective lysosomal enzymes cause storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs disease.
questions.explanation: The lysosomal membrane protects the cytoplasm from the enzymes; its failure triggers autolysis.

questions.question: Describe structure of mitochondria with suitable diagram.
questions.answer:
Mitochondria are rod-shaped or oval organelles, 0.5–1 µm wide and up to 10 µm long, bounded by two membranes.

Structure:
1. Outer membrane: smooth, permeable to small molecules, contains porin proteins.
2. Intermembrane space: narrow space between the two membranes; accumulates H⁺ during respiration.
3. Inner membrane: folded into finger-like cristae, which increase the surface area. It bears the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
4. Matrix: gel-like interior containing enzymes of the Krebs cycle, mitochondrial DNA (circular), 70S ribosomes and tRNA.

Diagram outline: label outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae, intermembrane space and matrix.

Functions: aerobic respiration, oxidation of pyruvate and fatty acids, ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation, calcium storage and apoptosis. Mitochondria are semi-autonomous because they contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
questions.explanation: The cristae increase the membrane area available for the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis.

questions.question: Explain the structure and composition of cell wall.
questions.answer:
Structure: the plant cell wall has three layers:
1. Middle lamella — the outermost layer between adjacent cells, made of calcium pectate; it glues cells together.
2. Primary wall — thin and elastic, laid down during growth; composed of cellulose microfibrils in a matrix of hemicellulose, pectin and water.
3. Secondary wall — thick and rigid, deposited inside the primary wall after growth stops; contains cellulose and lignin (in woody tissues).

Composition: cellulose (β-1,4-glucan) is the main structural fibre; hemicellulose, pectin, lignin, proteins and waxes (cutin) are also present. Plasmodesmata are channels that cross the wall and connect adjacent cells.

Functions: mechanical support and rigidity, protection, maintenance of turgor pressure, regulation of cell growth and transport, and defence against pathogens.
questions.explanation: The cell wall is fully permeable and non-living; it lies outside the plasma membrane.

questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of Golgi complex.
questions.answer:
Structure: the Golgi complex is a stack of 4–8 flattened, membrane-bound sacs (cisternae) surrounded by vesicles. It has a cis (forming) face, which receives vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum, and a trans (maturing) face, which releases vesicles toward the plasma membrane. It is well developed in secretory cells.

Functions:
1. Modification of proteins — glycosylation, phosphorylation and cutting of precursor proteins.
2. Sorting and packaging of proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport.
3. Secretion — forms secretory vesicles that release materials by exocytosis.
4. Formation of lysosomes and peroxisomes.
5. Synthesis of cell wall materials (pectin, hemicellulose) and glycoproteins in plant cells.
6. Membrane renewal and recycling.
7. Formation of the acrosome in sperm.

In plant cells the Golgi is called the dictyosome and is especially active in cell plate formation during cytokinesis.
questions.explanation: The Golgi is the cell's distribution centre, directing proteins to their correct destinations.

questions.question: Describe the types, structure, composition and functions of cytoskeleton.
questions.answer:
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments in the cytoplasm.

Types and composition:
1. Microtubules — hollow tubes about 25 nm diameter, made of tubulin (α and β) dimers. They form the spindle, centrioles, cilia and flagella and act as tracks for vesicle transport.
2. Microfilaments — solid fibres about 7 nm diameter, made of actin; they form networks and bundles, the contractile ring of dividing cells and the core of microvilli.
3. Intermediate filaments — about 10 nm diameter, made of proteins such as keratin, vimentin and lamin; they provide mechanical strength and anchor desmosomes.

Functions: maintain cell shape and support; anchor organelles; allow cell movement (amoeboid movement, cilia/flagella); muscle contraction (with myosin); intracellular transport of vesicles and organelles; chromosome movement during cell division; formation of cell junctions and the nuclear lamina.
questions.explanation: The three filament systems differ in size, protein composition and mechanical role, and cooperate in cell structure and movement.

questions.question: Why antenna complex contains other pigments with chlorophyll?
questions.answer: The antenna complex contains carotenoids and chlorophyll-b along with chlorophyll-a because these accessory pigments absorb wavelengths of light that chlorophyll-a absorbs poorly (especially blue-green and green-yellow regions). The absorbed energy is transferred by resonance to the reaction-centre chlorophyll-a. This broadens the range of the solar spectrum that can be used and protects chlorophyll from photo-oxidation.
questions.explanation: Accessory pigments act as light-harvesting aerials; only the reaction centre actually loses an electron.

questions.question: Why photosynthesis is called redox process?
questions.answer: Photosynthesis is a redox (oxidation-reduction) process because it involves transfer of electrons and hydrogen. In the light reaction, water is oxidized to O₂ (loss of electrons) while NADP⁺ is reduced to NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, CO₂ is reduced to carbohydrate while NADPH is oxidized. Since oxidation and reduction occur together, the overall process is a redox reaction.
questions.explanation: The light reaction is the reducing phase; the Calvin cycle is the carbon-fixing (reduction) phase.

questions.question: How cyclic photophosphorylation helpful in photosynthesis?
questions.answer: Cyclic photophosphorylation is useful because it produces extra ATP without consuming water or producing NADPH. It operates when the cell needs more ATP than NADPH, for example to supply the Calvin cycle or to maintain the proton gradient. It also protects the photosystems from over-reduction under low CO₂ conditions. Only PSI is involved and the electron returns to PSI.
questions.explanation: Cyclic flow generates ATP only; non-cyclic flow produces both ATP and NADPH.

questions.question: Why ATP is called common energy currency of living system?
questions.answer: ATP is called the common energy currency of the cell because it is the universal intermediate that links energy-releasing reactions with energy-requiring reactions. It is produced in respiration and photosynthesis, and its terminal phosphate bond is readily hydrolysed to release energy for muscular contraction, active transport, synthesis of molecules and other cellular work. It can be regenerated repeatedly, so it circulates like money in an economy.
questions.explanation: ATP is a short-term energy store; its level is kept steady by continuous synthesis and hydrolysis.

questions.question: Why Calvin cycle is also called C3 cycle?
questions.answer: The Calvin cycle is called the C3 cycle because the first stable product of CO₂ fixation is 3-phosphoglycerate, a 3-carbon compound. CO₂ is accepted by the 5-carbon RuBP, and the 6-carbon intermediate immediately splits into two 3-carbon molecules. Since the first detectable stable product contains three carbon atoms, the pathway is known as the C3 pathway.
questions.explanation: C3 refers to the first stable product, not to the number of carbons in CO₂.

questions.question: Why CAM plant close stomata in day time?
questions.answer: CAM (Crassulacean acid metabolism) plants close their stomata during the day to reduce water loss by transpiration in hot, dry habitats. Because the stomata are shut, CO₂ cannot enter by day, so these plants fix CO₂ at night, when stomata open and temperatures are lower. The CO₂ is stored as malic acid in vacuoles overnight and released to the Calvin cycle during the day.
questions.explanation: This temporal separation of CO₂ uptake and carbon fixation is the defining feature of CAM plants.

questions.question: Why oxidation of pyruvate provide more energy than lactic acid fermentation?
questions.answer: Pyruvate oxidation leads to the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain, where the acetyl group is completely oxidized to CO₂ and water. This yields about 30 ATP per glucose from NADH, FADH₂ and substrate-level phosphorylation. Lactic acid fermentation stops at lactate, an incompletely oxidized product, and yields only the 2 net ATP of glycolysis. Hence aerobic oxidation of pyruvate provides far more energy.
questions.explanation: Complete oxidation releases the remaining chemical energy stored in pyruvate's C–H bonds.

questions.question: Explain in detail light independent phase of photosynthesis.
questions.answer:
The light-independent phase (Calvin cycle, dark reaction) occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast. It uses the ATP and NADPH produced in the light reaction to reduce CO₂ into carbohydrate. It has three stages:

1. Carbon fixation: CO₂ combines with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C) in a reaction catalysed by rubisco, forming an unstable 6C compound that splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA, 3C).

2. Reduction: each 3-PGA is phosphorylated by ATP to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and then reduced by NADPH to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). Some G3P leaves the cycle to form glucose and other sugars.

3. Regeneration of RuBP: the remaining G3P molecules are rearranged through a series of reactions using ATP, regenerating RuBP so the cycle can continue.

Overall, three turns of the cycle fix three CO₂ and yield one G3P; two G3P make one glucose. The reaction does not require light directly but depends on the ATP and NADPH from the light reaction.
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle is called light-independent because its enzymes do not absorb light, not because it runs in darkness.

questions.question: What is cellular respiration? Explain types of respiration in detail.
questions.answer:
Cellular respiration is the stepwise oxidation of organic food molecules (mainly glucose) inside cells to release energy, which is trapped as ATP, with CO₂ and water as waste products. The overall equation is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (about 30 ATP).

Types:
1. Aerobic respiration — requires oxygen. Glucose is broken down in four stages: glycolysis (cytoplasm), pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix), Krebs cycle (matrix) and oxidative phosphorylation/electron transport chain (inner membrane). It completely oxidizes glucose and yields about 30 ATP per molecule.

2. Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) — occurs without oxygen. Only glycolysis operates, and pyruvate is converted to lactate or ethanol and CO₂ to regenerate NAD⁺. It yields only 2 ATP per glucose. Examples are lactic acid fermentation in muscles and in bacteria used for yoghurt, and alcoholic fermentation in yeast.

Anaerobic respiration in some bacteria uses nitrate or sulphate as the final electron acceptor and yields more ATP than fermentation but less than aerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Fermentation is not a separate pathway for energy production; it is a way of recycling NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

questions.question: Explain event takes place in breaking of glucose in cytosol.
questions.answer:
The breakdown of glucose in the cytosol is glycolysis, which occurs in ten enzyme-catalysed steps and does not require oxygen.

1. Glucose is phosphorylated by ATP to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase).
2. It is isomerized to fructose-6-phosphate.
3. Phosphofructokinase uses a second ATP to form fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
4. The 6C sugar is split by aldolase into two 3C molecules: dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (DHAP → G3P).
5. Each G3P is oxidized and phosphorylated to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, reducing NAD⁺ to NADH.
6. Two ATP are formed as 1,3-BPG is converted to 3-phosphoglycerate (substrate-level phosphorylation).
7. 3-PGA is converted to 2-phosphoglycerate and then to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP).
8. Pyruvate kinase transfers the phosphate of PEP to ADP, forming a second ATP per 3C molecule and releasing pyruvate.

Overall: one glucose → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH. The two pyruvate molecules then enter the mitochondrion for pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle under aerobic conditions.
questions.explanation: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and produces 4 ATP, giving a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.

questions.question: Discuss cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation during light reaction.
questions.answer:
Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP using light energy in the chloroplast.

Cyclic photophosphorylation:
- Only PSI is involved; the electron is excited by light and passes to ferredoxin, then through cytochrome b₆f and back to PSI.
- The electron travels in a cycle, so no NADPH is formed and water is not split.
- A proton gradient is created, which drives ATP synthase to form ATP.
- It occurs mainly in stroma lamellae under low light or when NADPH is not needed.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation:
- Both PSII and PSI cooperate in a linear (Z) scheme.
- PSII absorbs light, loses electrons and splits water (photolysis) to replace them, releasing O₂ and protons.
- Electrons pass through the electron transport chain, generating a proton gradient and ATP.
- PSI re-excites the electrons, which reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH via ferredoxin and NADP reductase.
- Both ATP and NADPH are produced, and water is consumed.

In photosynthesis both processes usually run together: non-cyclic flow supplies NADPH and ATP for the Calvin cycle, while cyclic flow supplies additional ATP.
questions.explanation: The proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is common to both pathways and drives ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.

questions.question: Describes tricarboxylic acid cycle in detail.
questions.answer:
The tricarboxylic acid (TCA)/Krebs/citric acid cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix and oxidizes acetyl-CoA to CO₂, generating NADH, FADH₂ and GTP.

Steps (per acetyl-CoA):
1. Acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C) by citrate synthase.
2. Citrate is isomerized through cis-aconitate to isocitrate.
3. Isocitrate is oxidatively decarboxylated to α-ketoglutarate (5C), releasing CO₂ and forming NADH.
4. α-ketoglutarate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to succinyl-CoA (4C), releasing CO₂ and forming NADH.
5. Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate, forming GTP (ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation.
6. Succinate is oxidized to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH₂.
7. Fumarate is hydrated to malate.
8. Malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate, reducing NAD⁺ to NADH; oxaloacetate is ready for the next cycle.

Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂. Per glucose (two turns): 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 GTP and 4 CO₂. The NADH and FADH₂ are then oxidized by the electron transport chain.
questions.explanation: The cycle is amphibolic: it also supplies intermediates for amino acids, fatty acids and haem synthesis.

questions.question: Explain alternative mechanism of CO₂ fixation in plant.
questions.answer:
Some plants avoid photorespiration and water loss by alternative CO₂ fixation pathways.

C4 pathway (Hatch–Slack):
- Occurs in grasses such as maize, sugarcane and sorghum.
- CO₂ is fixed in mesophyll cells by PEP carboxylase onto phosphoenolpyruvate, forming oxaloacetate (4C), which is reduced to malate.
- Malate moves to bundle-sheath cells, where it is decarboxylated, releasing CO₂ to the Calvin cycle and forming pyruvate.
- Pyruvate returns to the mesophyll and is regenerated to PEP at the cost of ATP.
- Because PEP carboxylase has no oxygenase activity and CO₂ is concentrated around rubisco, photorespiration is minimized. The anatomy shows Kranz structure.

CAM pathway:
- Occurs in succulents such as cactus, pineapple and Bryophyllum.
- Stomata open at night, when CO₂ is fixed by PEP carboxylase into oxaloacetate and stored as malic acid in vacuoles.
- During the day stomata close to conserve water and malic acid is decarboxylated; the released CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle.

Both pathways separate CO₂ supply from the Calvin cycle and reduce photorespiration.
questions.explanation: C4 separates the two steps in space (mesophyll vs bundle sheath); CAM separates them in time (night vs day).

questions.question: Explain chemiosmosis and oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.answer:
Chemiosmosis is the mechanism by which the energy of an electron transport chain is used to make ATP through a proton gradient across a membrane.

Process:
1. As electrons pass along the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane, protons (H⁺) are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space by complexes I, III and IV.
2. This creates an electrochemical gradient (proton motive force) — high H⁺ concentration and positive charge in the intermembrane space.
3. Protons return to the matrix through the channel of ATP synthase (F₀ portion), and the flow drives rotation of the enzyme and phosphorylation of ADP to ATP at the F₁ portion.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the overall process in which NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain, oxygen accepts them at the end to form water, and ATP is synthesized by chemiosmosis. NADH enters at complex I (3 ATP) and FADH₂ at complex II (2 ATP). About 26–28 ATP are produced per glucose. The process is called oxidative because the food-derived carriers are oxidized, and phosphorylation because ADP is phosphorylated.
questions.explanation: The proton gradient, not a direct chemical transfer, links electron transport to ATP synthesis; uncouplers such as DNP dissipate the gradient and stop ATP production.

questions.question: Viruses evolve by using the
questions.answer: (d) All of them
questions.explanation: Viruses have no metabolism of their own. For replication and evolution they use the host cell's organelles (ribosomes, membranes), enzymes (polymerases) and energy (ATP), so all of them are used.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Cellular organelles  (b) Cellular enzymes  (c) Cellular energy  (d) All of them

questions.question: The pathogenicity of a virus depends upon
questions.answer: (b) the effective penetration of its genome
questions.explanation: A virus causes disease only if its genome successfully penetrates the host cell and is expressed there. Host immunity and environment modify the outcome, but the primary determinant of pathogenicity is effective genome penetration and replication.

options.text: the immunity of the host body
the effective penetration of its genome
the overall environment inside the body
the overall environment outside the body

questions.optionsRaw: (a) the immunity of the host body  (b) the effective penetration of its genome  (c) the overall environment inside the body  (d) the overall environment outside the body

questions.answer: (a) Lysozyme
questions.explanation: Phage-infected bacteria produce lysozyme (endolysin) which digests the peptidoglycan of the bacterial cell wall, causing the cell to burst and release new phages.

questions.explanation: During assembly (maturation) viral proteins are cut into functional units and packaged with the nucleic acid into complete new virions. Integration and transcription concern the genome, while budding is a mode of release.

questions.question: Virus that severely damage motor neurons and causes paralysis called
questions.answer: (c) Polio
questions.explanation: Poliovirus invades the central nervous system and destroys motor neurons in the spinal cord, producing flaccid paralysis.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) HIV  (b) Dengue  (c) Polio  (d) Herpes

questions.answer: (a) Prions
questions.explanation: Prions are infectious misfolded proteins (e.g. PrP^Sc) that cause degenerative brain diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and mad cow disease. They contain no nucleic acid.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Prions  (b) Viroids  (c) Antigen  (d) Antibodies

questions.answer: (b) Viroids
questions.explanation: Viroids are naked, circular, single-stranded RNA molecules smaller than viruses, with some double-stranded regions formed by base pairing. They cause plant diseases such as potato spindle tuber disease.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Prions  (b) Viroids  (c) Minus strand viruses  (d) Double stranded DNA viruses

questions.answer: (a) Arbo-viruses
questions.explanation: Arboviruses (arthropod-borne viruses) are transmitted by mosquitoes or ticks and include the dengue, yellow fever and encephalitis viruses.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Arbo-viruses  (b) Retro-viruses  (c) Rhabdo-viruses  (d) Rhino-viruses

questions.answer: (a) Dengue virus
questions.explanation: Dengue virus is transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which bite mainly during the day.
