questions.question: Why higher animals need circulatory system?
questions.answer: Higher animals are large and multicellular, so most of their cells lie far from the external environment. Diffusion alone is too slow over such distances — the time required for a substance to diffuse is proportional to the square of the distance it must travel. A circulatory system solves this problem by keeping the distance from blood to any cell very short: it transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and water to the tissues and carries carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes away to the lungs, kidneys and other excretory organs. It also distributes heat for temperature regulation and carries white blood cells and antibodies for defence. In this way the circulatory system functionally connects the aqueous environment of the cells with the organs that exchange gases, absorb nutrients and dispose of wastes.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.1: diffusion is inadequate over macroscopic distances; the circulatory system ensures no substance must diffuse far to enter or leave a cell.

questions.question: Why SA node is called pace maker of heart?
questions.answer: The sino-atrial (SA) node is a small region of specialized muscle tissue in the wall of the right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava. It generates electrical impulses spontaneously and rhythmically, without any external nerve stimulation, at a rate of about 72 times per minute at rest. These impulses spread rapidly through the walls of both atria, making them contract together, and then pass to the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres to excite the ventricles. Because the SA node sets the rate and rhythm at which all cardiac muscle cells contract, it is called the pacemaker of the heart. If it is damaged, the AV node can take over as a slower backup pacemaker.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.3.3 (SA node and AV node).

questions.question: Why the capillaries have a single layer of endothelium?
questions.answer: Capillaries are the site of exchange between blood and tissue fluid, so their wall is reduced to the minimum thickness: a single layer of squamous endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane. This thin wall offers very little resistance to diffusion, allowing oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, water and wastes to pass rapidly between the blood and the interstitial fluid. The capillaries are also extremely narrow (7–9 µm), which slows the blood flow and gives more time for exchange, and their walls have openings between cells through which white blood cells can squeeze out. A thicker wall would increase the diffusion distance and make exchange inefficient.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.5.2 (capillaries).

questions.question: What are LUB and DUB?
questions.answer: LUB and DUB are the two heart sounds heard through a stethoscope as 'lub-dub'. LUB is the first, longer and lower-pitched sound. It is produced by the sudden closure of the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid/mitral) at the beginning of ventricular systole, when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and the valve flaps are forced shut. DUB is the second, shorter and sharper sound. It is caused by the closure of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) at the end of ventricular systole, when blood starts to flow back toward the relaxing ventricles and closes the valve cusps. The sounds are due to vibrations of the heart walls and valves, not to the flow of blood itself.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.3.2 (phases of heartbeat).

questions.question: Why circulatory system of arthropods is called open type?
questions.answer: In arthropods the circulatory system is called open because the blood (haemolymph) is not confined to a continuous system of vessels. The tubular heart pumps haemolymph through short arteries into irregular spaces called sinuses or the haemocoel, where it directly bathes the internal organs and cells. It is then collected back into the heart through openings called ostia. Because the haemolymph leaves the vessels and mixes with the interstitial fluid, there is no distinction between blood and tissue fluid, and the system operates at low pressure. Open circulation is adequate for small animals with relatively low metabolic rates, but it is less efficient than closed circulation for rapid transport of oxygen and nutrients.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.1 (open circulatory system).

questions.question: Why blood flow faster in arteries?
questions.answer: Blood flows faster in arteries because it is driven by the high pressure generated by ventricular contraction and because arteries have a relatively small total cross-sectional area. The thick muscular and elastic walls of arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining a high pressure and pushing blood onward between heartbeats. Since the velocity of flow is inversely related to the total cross-sectional area of the vessels, blood moves rapidly through the narrow arterial tree; as the arteries branch into many arterioles and then into an enormous number of capillaries, the total cross-sectional area increases greatly and the flow slows down, allowing time for exchange. In veins, by contrast, pressure is low, walls are thin and the lumen is wider, so flow is slower and depends on valves and skeletal-muscle pumping.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 12.5.1 (arteries) and 12.5.3 (veins).

questions.question: Distinguish between single circuit circulation and double circuit circulation:
questions.answer: In single circuit circulation, blood passes through the heart only once during one complete circuit of the body. The heart has two chambers (one atrium and one ventricle), as in fish. Deoxygenated blood is pumped from the heart to the gills, where it is oxygenated, and then flows directly through the body tissues before returning to the heart. The blood loses pressure in the gill capillaries, so the systemic circulation is at low pressure and the tissues receive blood relatively slowly. In double circuit circulation, blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit: once through the pulmonary circuit (heart → lungs → heart) and once through the systemic circuit (heart → body → heart). The heart has three chambers in amphibians and most reptiles and four chambers in birds and mammals. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are separated (completely in birds and mammals), so the systemic circulation can be maintained at high pressure and oxygen delivery to the tissues is more efficient.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.2 (evolution of vertebrate heart and double circulation).

questions.question: Describe the structure of blood vessels in man.
questions.answer:
The blood vessels of man form a continuous system of tubes of three main types — arteries, capillaries and veins — through which blood travels from the heart to the tissues and back.

1. Arteries. Arteries are thick-walled vessels that carry blood away from the heart. Their wall consists of three layers (tunics). The outer tunica externa is made of fibrous connective tissue containing collagen fibres, giving strength. The middle tunica media is the thickest layer and contains smooth muscle and elastic fibres; it allows the artery to stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining a steady flow of blood. The inner tunica intima consists of a single layer of squamous endothelium, which provides a smooth lining. Arteries have a narrow lumen and no valves. They branch into smaller vessels called arterioles, whose muscular walls can constrict or dilate to control the distribution of blood and peripheral resistance.

2. Capillaries. Capillaries are the smallest vessels, connecting arterioles to venules. Their wall is only one cell thick — a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane — and their diameter is about 7–9 µm, just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file. This thin wall allows rapid exchange of gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes between blood and interstitial fluid. Capillaries form dense networks in the tissues. The large plasma proteins, red blood cells and platelets cannot leave the capillaries, but white blood cells can pass through openings between the endothelial cells.

3. Veins and venules. Venules collect blood from the capillary networks and join to form veins, which return blood to the heart. Veins have thinner walls than arteries, with less smooth muscle and elastic tissue, and a wider lumen, so they offer little resistance to flow. Blood pressure in veins is low, so veins contain one-way valves that prevent backflow; the contraction of skeletal muscles during exercise and the movements of breathing squeeze the veins and help push blood toward the heart. The largest veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, empty into the right atrium.

Thus arteries are adapted for high-pressure transport away from the heart, capillaries for exchange, and veins for low-pressure return of blood to the heart.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.5 (blood vessels: arteries, capillaries, veins; Fig. 12.7).

questions.question: Describe the structure of human heart.
questions.answer:
The human heart is a hollow, somewhat conical muscular organ about the size of a fist. It lies in the thorax between the lungs, behind the sternum, with about one third of its mass to the right of the midline and two thirds to the left.

Pericardium. The heart is enclosed in a tough sac called the pericardium. It has an outer fibrous layer (fibrous pericardium) and an inner double serous membrane (serous pericardium). Between the two layers of the serous pericardium is a small amount of pericardial fluid, which lubricates the surfaces and prevents friction during heart contractions.

Wall of the heart. The heart wall consists of three layers. The epicardium is the outer layer, formed by the visceral layer of the serous pericardium. The myocardium is the thick middle layer of cardiac muscle; it contains the excitable tissue and the conducting system of the heart and is responsible for the pumping action. The endocardium is the inner layer, consisting of squamous endothelium and a subendocardial layer, which lines the chambers and valves.

Chambers. Internally the heart is divided into four chambers: two thin-walled atria above and two thick-walled ventricles below. The right and left atria are separated by a thin membranous interatrial septum, and the right and left ventricles by a thick muscular interventricular septum. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins. The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk, and the left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta. The wall of the left ventricle is much thicker than that of the right because it must drive blood through the systemic circulation, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

Valves. Four valves ensure one-way flow. The right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve lies between the right atrium and ventricle, and the left atrioventricular (bicuspid or mitral) valve between the left atrium and ventricle. Their flaps are anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, which prevent the valves from turning inside out during ventricular contraction. The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the opening of the pulmonary trunk, and the aortic semilunar valve guards the opening of the aorta.

Great vessels. The superior and inferior venae cavae enter the right atrium; the pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries; four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium; and the aorta leaves the left ventricle and arches over the heart. The heart also has its own coronary arteries and veins, which supply and drain the myocardium.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 12.3, 12.3.1 and Fig. 12.3–12.4.

questions.question: What is circulation? Explain needs of circulation
questions.answer:
Circulation is the movement of blood (or another body fluid) through the body, driven by a heart or other pumping structures, so that substances are transported between the exchange organs and the cells. In animals there are two basic types: open circulation, in which haemolymph leaves the vessels and directly bathes the organs, and closed circulation, in which blood remains confined to vessels and is distinct from the interstitial fluid. Man has a closed, double circulatory system.

The need for circulation arises from the size and complexity of multicellular animals. In a unicellular organism or a very small animal, diffusion alone is sufficient to supply oxygen and nutrients and remove wastes. In a large animal, however, most cells are far from the body surface and from the gut, and the time taken for diffusion is proportional to the square of the distance. Diffusion would therefore be far too slow to meet metabolic demands. Circulation solves this problem by keeping the distance between blood and each cell very short and by continuously renewing the fluid around the cells.

Specifically, circulation is needed for:
1. Transport of respiratory gases — oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs.
2. Transport of nutrients — glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals and water absorbed from the digestive tract to all cells.
3. Transport of metabolic wastes — urea, uric acid, creatinine, excess salts and water — to the kidneys and other excretory organs.
4. Transport of hormones from endocrine glands to their target organs, and of enzymes and plasma proteins.
5. Distribution of heat, helping to regulate body temperature and maintain a constant internal environment (homeostasis).
6. Defence — carrying white blood cells, antibodies and clotting factors to sites of injury or infection.
7. Maintaining the composition of interstitial fluid, so that tissue cells are bathed in a suitable medium for metabolism.

Thus circulation functionally connects the aqueous environment of the cells with the organs that exchange gases, absorb nutrients and dispose of wastes. Without it, the metabolic rate and size of higher animals would be severely limited.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 12.1 and 12.2 (circulation, types and needs).

questions.question: State the phases of heartbeat in man.
questions.answer:
The heartbeat is the rhythmic contraction of the heart chambers. At rest the human heart beats about 72 times per minute, so one complete cardiac cycle — one contraction and relaxation of the atria and ventricles — lasts about 0.8 second. The cycle has three main phases.

1. Atrial systole (about 0.1 s). The SA node fires, and electrical impulses spread through the walls of both atria, causing them to contract together. The atrioventricular valves are open, so blood is forced from the atria into the ventricles, which are relaxed and filling.

2. Ventricular systole (about 0.3 s). The impulse passes through the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres to the ventricular muscle. The ventricles contract, raising the pressure inside them. This closes the atrioventricular valves, producing the first heart sound (LUB), and then opens the semilunar valves. Blood is ejected into the pulmonary trunk from the right ventricle and into the aorta from the left ventricle. During this phase the atria relax and begin to fill again.

3. Ventricular diastole (about 0.5 s). The ventricles relax, their pressure falls, and the semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound (DUB). The atrioventricular valves then open, and blood flows from the atria into the ventricles. This is a period of complete cardiac relaxation before the next atrial systole begins. The coronary arteries are also filled during diastole, when the ventricular muscle is relaxed.

The alternating contraction and relaxation of the chambers, together with the opening and closing of the valves, therefore maintain a continuous one-way flow of blood through the heart. The sequence repeats with each heartbeat.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.3.2 (phases of heartbeat; Fig. 12.5).

questions.question: Describe the flow of blood through human heart as regulated by the valves.
questions.answer:
Blood flows through the human heart in a definite one-way path, and the four heart valves ensure that it never flows backward.

Deoxygenated blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae. When the right atrium contracts, the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve opens and blood passes into the right ventricle. During ventricular systole the tricuspid valve closes, preventing blood from being forced back into the right atrium; its flaps are held in place by chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles. The pressure in the right ventricle opens the pulmonary semilunar valve, and blood is ejected into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

In the lungs the blood is oxygenated and returns to the left atrium through the four pulmonary veins. When the left atrium contracts, the left atrioventricular (bicuspid or mitral) valve opens and blood enters the left ventricle. During left ventricular systole the bicuspid valve closes, preventing backflow into the left atrium. The rising ventricular pressure opens the aortic semilunar valve, and blood is ejected into the aorta and distributed to the body.

The valves work purely passively, opening and closing in response to pressure differences on their two sides:
- Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) are open when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure (during atrial filling and atrial systole) and are closed when ventricular pressure rises during ventricular systole.
- Semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) are closed when ventricular pressure falls during diastole, preventing blood in the great arteries from flowing back into the ventricles; they open only when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure during systole.

The closing of the AV valves produces the first heart sound (LUB), and the closing of the semilunar valves produces the second heart sound (DUB). In this way the valves maintain the sequence: right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body, with no backward leakage at any step.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 12.3.1 and 12.3.2 (heart valves and the cardiac cycle).

questions.question: Describe the lymphatic system of man
questions.answer:
The lymphatic system is a network of thin-walled vessels and lymphoid organs that returns excess tissue fluid to the blood and helps defend the body against infection.

Formation of lymph. All body tissues are bathed in interstitial (tissue) fluid, which is formed when blood passes through the capillaries. About 85% of this fluid returns into the blood at the venous end of the capillaries; the remaining 15% drains into blind-ended lymphatic capillaries as lymph. Lymph is a colourless fluid containing lymphocytes, small proteins, fats, cell debris and microorganisms. It also carries substances that are too large to penetrate the blood capillaries, such as fat globules absorbed from the villi of the small intestine.

Lymph capillaries and vessels. Lymph capillaries are microscopically narrow, thin-walled vessels with openings between their cells that act as one-way valves, allowing relatively large particles and fluid to enter. They join to form larger lymph vessels, which have somewhat muscular walls and numerous one-way valves. Lymph is propelled mainly by the contraction of nearby skeletal muscles during breathing and walking, and the valves prevent backflow. The larger vessels merge into two ducts: the thoracic duct, which drains most of the body and empties into the left subclavian vein, and the right lymphatic duct, which drains the right side of the head, thorax and right arm and empties into the right subclavian vein.

Lymphoid organs. Lymph vessels are interrupted at intervals by kidney-bean-shaped lymph nodes, about one inch long. Lymph is forced through channels lined with macrophages, and lymphocytes are also produced in the nodes; both types of white blood cells recognise and destroy foreign particles such as bacteria and viruses. The spleen, located on the left side of the abdominal cavity between the stomach and diaphragm, filters blood and exposes it to macrophages and lymphocytes that destroy foreign particles and aged red blood cells. The thymus is a lymphoid organ in the upper chest where T lymphocytes mature, and the tonsils are masses of lymphoid tissue guarding the throat.

Functions. The lymphatic system (1) returns excess interstitial fluid and small proteins to the blood, maintaining fluid balance; (2) transports absorbed fats from the intestine; (3) filters lymph and blood and destroys pathogens and worn-out cells; and (4) produces and distributes lymphocytes for immune defence. If lymph drainage is blocked, interstitial fluid accumulates and causes swelling called oedema.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.8 (lymphatic system; Figs. 12.13–12.14).

questions.question: Explain the electrocardiogram with the help of diagram.
questions.answer:
An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a graphic record of the electrical currents produced by the heart during the cardiac cycle. The impulses that travel through cardiac muscle produce electrical currents, which are conducted through body fluids to the body surface. These currents are detected by electrodes placed on the skin and are recorded as a trace called an ECG.

A normal ECG consists of a repeating sequence of waves (P, QRS and T) on a baseline:
- P wave: a small upward wave produced by depolarization of the atrial muscle fibres, initiated by the SA node. It represents atrial depolarization, which is followed by atrial contraction.
- P–R interval: the time from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex. It indicates the time required for the depolarization initiated by the SA node to reach the ventricles, and therefore reflects conduction through the AV node (normally about 0.1 s).
- QRS complex: a sharp downward deflection (Q), a tall upward spike (R) and a downward deflection (S). It represents depolarization of the ventricles, which begins at the apex of the heart and spreads upward. Atrial repolarization also occurs during this time but is hidden by the larger QRS complex.
- S–T segment: the period between the end of ventricular depolarization and the beginning of repolarization. During this interval the ventricles are in systole and blood is being ejected from the heart.
- T wave: a broader upward wave produced by ventricular repolarization, which occurs just before the ventricles relax.

Diagram (described): draw a horizontal baseline; add a small rounded P wave, followed after a short flat P–R segment by a tall sharp QRS spike (small Q dip, tall R peak, S dip below baseline), then a flat S–T segment, and finally a broader rounded T wave. The sequence P–QRS–T repeats with each heartbeat.

By examining the ECG, a physician can see the electrical changes in the form of depolarization and repolarization and can detect abnormalities such as irregular rhythm, heart block, myocardial damage or hypertrophy. A normal ECG indicates that the heart is functioning and conducting impulses properly.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 12.4 (electrocardiogram; Figs. 12.6 and ECG waves).

questions.question: Describe pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation
questions.answer:
In man the circulatory system is a double circuit: blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit of the body. The two circuits are the pulmonary circulation and the systemic circulation.

Pulmonary circulation. This circuit carries deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs and returns oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart. Blood enters the right atrium from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary trunk. The trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry blood to the two lungs. In the pulmonary capillaries, carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood into the alveoli and oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood. The oxygenated blood then returns through four pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The pulmonary circuit is short and operates at low pressure, which protects the delicate lung capillaries from damage.

Systemic circulation. This circuit carries oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart to all body tissues and returns deoxygenated blood to the right side. Blood passes from the left atrium through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic semilunar valve into the aorta. The aorta branches into arteries and arterioles that distribute blood to the head, limbs, trunk and internal organs. In the tissue capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass into the cells, while carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes enter the blood. The deoxygenated blood then flows through venules and veins and returns to the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae. The systemic circuit is long and operates at high pressure, because the left ventricle has a thick muscular wall. The coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle itself, are also part of the systemic circulation.

Thus pulmonary circulation oxygenates the blood at low pressure, while systemic circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients to the tissues and removes wastes at high pressure. Together they ensure that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood remain separate in the four-chambered human heart, making oxygen delivery to the tissues highly efficient.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 12.2 and 12.3 (double circulation, pulmonary and systemic circuits).

questions.question: The study of functioning and disorders of immune system is termed as:
questions.answer: (c) Immunology
questions.explanation: Immunology is the branch of biology that deals with the structure and function of the immune system and with its disorders. Immunity is the resistance of the body to infection, while an immune response is the reaction of the immune system to an antigen.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Immunity  (b) Immune response  (c) Immunology  (d) all of these

questions.question: It is responsible for specific immune response:
questions.answer: (d) Third line of defense
questions.explanation: The third line of defence is the specific (adaptive) immune system. It is mediated by T and B lymphocytes, recognises particular antigens and produces a tailored response with immunological memory. The first and second lines are non-specific and act against all pathogens in the same way.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Innate Immune system  (b) First line of defense  (c) Second line of defense  (d) Third line of defense

questions.question: Following serves as physical barrier:
questions.answer: (b) Mucous membrane
questions.explanation: A mucous membrane is a physical barrier that lines the respiratory, digestive and reproductive tracts and prevents the entry of pathogens. Macrophages are cellular defenders, while HCl and saliva are biochemical barriers.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Macrophage  (b) Mucous membrane  (c) HCl  (d) Saliva

questions.question: Our digestive tract consists of what kind of barriers?
questions.answer: (c) Both a & b
questions.explanation: The digestive tract has physical barriers (the intact mucosa with its tightly packed epithelial cells and the washing action of peristalsis) and biochemical barriers (HCl and enzymes of gastric juice, mucus containing antimicrobial peptides, and saliva). Together they form the first line of defence.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Physical barriers  (b) Biochemical barriers  (c) Both a & b  (d) None of these

questions.question: Which of the following is involved in phagocytosis of bacteria?
questions.answer: (c) Both a & b
questions.explanation: Both neutrophils and macrophages are professional phagocytes. Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and are specially adapted to engulf bacteria, while macrophages are long-lived tissue phagocytes derived from monocytes. Dendritic cells are also phagocytic.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Neutrophil  (b) Macrophage  (c) Both a & b  (d) None of these

questions.question: It is not involved in antigen presentation:
questions.answer: (c) Neutrophil
questions.explanation: Macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells are antigen-presenting cells (APCs) because they display processed antigen on MHC-II to helper T cells. Neutrophils are phagocytes but are not regarded as antigen-presenting cells.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Macrophage  (b) Dendritic cell  (c) Neutrophil  (d) Both a & b

questions.question: The type of receptor exhibited by all nucleated cells other than macrophages is:
questions.answer: (a) MHC-I
questions.explanation: MHC-I molecules are expressed on the plasma membrane of almost all nucleated cells and act as a universal 'self' identification card. MHC-II is restricted mainly to antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells. TCR is the antigen receptor of T cells.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) MHC-I  (b) MHC-II  (c) Both a & b  (d) TCR

questions.question: Any foreign substance that can elicit immune response is called:
questions.answer: (b) Antigen
questions.explanation: An antigen is any foreign macromolecule, usually a protein or polysaccharide, that is recognised as non-self and provokes an immune response. An antibody is a protein produced by plasma cells that binds specifically to an antigen; an antihistamine is a drug used against allergic reactions.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Antibody  (b) Antigen  (c) Both a & c  (d) Antihistamine

questions.question: The type of immunity through the transfer of antibodies from mother to her fetus is:
questions.answer: (b) Natural Passive Immunity
questions.explanation: Antibodies (mainly IgG) cross the placenta from mother to fetus, and antibodies are also passed in breast milk. The baby receives ready-made antibodies without producing them, so the immunity is passive, and because it occurs naturally it is called natural passive immunity.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) Natural Active Immunity  (b) Natural Passive Immunity  (c) Artificial Active Immunity  (d) Artificial Passive Immunity

questions.question: Antibodies are secreted by:
questions.answer: (c) Plasma cells
questions.explanation: When a B lymphocyte is activated by antigen and helper T-cell signals, it proliferates and differentiates into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory B cells. T cells do not secrete antibodies; macrophages are phagocytes.
questions.optionsRaw: (a) T cells  (b) B cells  (c) Plasma cells  (d) Macrophages

questions.question: List out any six biochemical barriers.
questions.answer:
The first line of defence includes biochemical barriers in the secretions that bathe the body surfaces. Six examples given in the textbook are:

1. Saliva — contains lysozyme and antibodies that destroy bacteria and washes microbes from the mouth.
2. Mucus — a sticky secretion that traps microorganisms and contains antimicrobial peptides.
3. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) — secreted by the gastric glands; its very low pH kills most swallowed pathogens.
4. Gastric juice — contains HCl and digestive enzymes that together destroy microorganisms in the stomach.
5. Tears — contain lysozyme and wash microbes away from the surface of the eye.
6. Spermine — an antimicrobial substance present in semen.

Sweat and sebum also contribute: sweat is salty and acidic, and sebum contains fatty acids that inhibit microbial growth.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.1 and Table 13.1 (biochemical barriers: saliva, mucus, HCl, gastric juice, tears, spermine).

questions.question: How the tumor cells are dealt with by our immune system?
questions.answer:
Tumour cells arise from the body's own cells but carry altered or abnormal surface molecules, so they are treated as non-self by the immune system — a process called immune surveillance. They are dealt with mainly by cytotoxicity:

1. Natural killer (NK) cells patrol the tissues and recognise cells that have lost or altered their MHC-I molecules ('missing self'), which is common in tumour cells. NK cells release perforin, which punches pores in the tumour cell membrane, and granzymes, which enter and trigger apoptosis.
2. Cytotoxic T (Tc) cells recognise tumour-specific antigens displayed on MHC-I and kill the target cell by releasing perforin and granzymes and by signals such as Fas ligand. They also secrete cytokines such as interferon-γ and tumour necrosis factor-α.
3. Macrophages and dendritic cells phagocytose tumour debris and present tumour antigens to helper T cells, which in turn activate Tc cells and B cells.
4. Antibodies produced by plasma cells can coat tumour cells, activate complement and promote their destruction by phagocytes (opsonisation).

Tumours can nevertheless escape by losing antigen expression, secreting immunosuppressive factors or suppressing tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes. This is why immunotherapy (for example monoclonal antibodies and checkpoint inhibitors) is used against cancers such as malignant melanoma.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 13.2.1 (cytotoxicity, NK and Tc cells) and the box on malignant melanoma; standard immunology added for the antibody/complement role.

questions.question: Differentiate between NK Cell and Tc cell.
questions.answer:
Both natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T (Tc) cells kill target cells, but they differ in origin of specificity, recognition and mode of action:

1. Specificity. NK cells are non-specific and belong to the innate immune system; they attack any cell that appears abnormal without prior sensitisation. Tc cells are specific and belong to the adaptive immune system; each clone recognises one particular antigen.
2. Receptor. NK cells have no T-cell receptor (TCR) and are not MHC-restricted. They carry activating and inhibitory receptors and kill when MHC-I is missing or altered ('missing self'). Tc cells carry a TCR and the CD8 marker and recognise antigen only when it is displayed on MHC-I ('MHC restriction').
3. Activation. NK cells are ready to act immediately and respond within hours. Tc cells must first be activated by antigen presentation and helper-T-cell cytokines, then proliferate and differentiate, so their response takes days.
4. Mechanism. Both release perforin (which forms pores) and granzymes (which trigger apoptosis). Tc cells also use Fas ligand and secrete IFN-γ and TNF-α. NK cells can additionally kill antibody-coated cells by ADCC.
5. Memory. Tc cells produce long-lived memory T cells, giving rapid protection on re-exposure. NK cells have little or no immunological memory.
6. Role. NK cells provide early defence against virus-infected and tumour cells; Tc cells provide specific, long-lasting killing of virus-infected cells, intracellular bacteria and tumour cells and are described as 'serial killers'.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.1 (cytotoxicity: NK cells and Tc cells).

questions.question: List out the ways of second line of defense.
questions.answer:
The second line of defence is non-specific and comes into play when the first line (skin and mucous membranes) is breached. Its ways are:

1. Phagocytosis — neutrophils, macrophages (derived from monocytes) and dendritic cells engulf and digest pathogens.
2. Cytotoxicity — natural killer (NK) cells destroy virus-infected and tumour cells by releasing perforin and granzymes.
3. Inflammation — a localised vascular and cellular response that brings phagocytes and antimicrobial substances to the site of injury or infection.
4. Fever — a raised body temperature that inhibits microbial growth and enhances phagocytosis and immune activity.
5. Antimicrobial proteins — complement proteins (which lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis) and interferons (which make surrounding cells resistant to viral infection).

These responses are rapid and act in the same way against all pathogens, but they do not provide immunological memory.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2 (second line of defence: phagocytosis, cytotoxicity, inflammation, fever and protective proteins).

questions.question: Even though the core proteins are the same, how antibodies differ from each other?
questions.answer:
All antibody molecules share the same basic 'core' or framework: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, held together by disulfide bonds and folded into constant and variable regions. They differ from one another in the following ways:

1. Variable regions. The tips of the heavy and light chains form the variable regions (VH and VL). Their amino-acid sequences are different in every antibody clone, and together they make the antigen-binding site. It is this variable part that gives each antibody its specificity for a particular antigen or epitope.
2. Antigen-binding site. Because the variable regions differ, one antibody may bind a bacterial surface protein, another a viral coat protein and another a pollen allergen. The shape of the binding site must be complementary to the epitope.
3. Class (isotype). Antibodies also differ in the constant region of their heavy chains, which defines five classes — IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. Each class has a different distribution and effector function (for example, IgA is secreted in mucous secretions and milk, IgE binds mast cells in allergy, IgM is a large pentamer).
4. Membrane versus secreted form. A B-cell receptor (BCR) is a membrane-bound antibody; after activation the same B cell may secrete a soluble form of the antibody.

Thus the constant 'core' carries out common effector functions, while variation in the variable regions (and in heavy-chain constant regions) makes antibodies diverse and specific.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.3.2 and Fig. 13.13 (BCR: light and heavy chains with variable and constant regions); antibody classes are standard immunology.

questions.question: What is antipyretic therapy and why it is used?
questions.answer:
Antipyretic therapy is the use of antipyretic drugs to reduce or control fever. Fever is produced when pyrogens stimulate the hypothalamus to secrete prostaglandins, which raise the body's temperature set point. Antipyretics lower the set point again by inhibiting the synthesis of prostaglandins — most of them inhibit the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX).

The three main groups are salicylates (aspirin), acetaminophen (paracetamol) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen).

Antipyretic therapy is used because a high fever is uncomfortable and can be harmful. It relieves headache, body ache, fatigue and malaise, reduces fluid loss and dehydration, prevents febrile seizures, especially in children, and avoids damage to enzymes and brain cells when temperature rises above about 105°F. It is a symptomatic treatment: it makes the patient comfortable but does not eradicate the underlying infection, so the cause must still be diagnosed and treated.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.4 and the antipyretic-drugs box.

questions.question: List out four autoimmune disorders of man.
questions.answer:
In autoimmune disorders the immune system fails to recognise the body's own tissues as self and produces antibodies or T cells that attack them. Four examples are:

1. Type-1 diabetes mellitus — autoantibodies and cytotoxic T cells destroy the insulin-secreting β-cells of the islets of Langerhans, so insulin must be injected.
2. Rheumatoid arthritis — autoimmune inflammation of the synovial membranes of joints, with destruction of cartilage and bone and progressive joint deformity.
3. Psoriasis — an autoimmune skin disorder in which T cells stimulate rapid proliferation of skin cells, producing thick, scaly, red plaques.
4. Multiple sclerosis — autoimmune destruction of the myelin sheath of nerve fibres in the central nervous system, causing weakness, numbness and coordination problems.

Other examples include myasthenia gravis and systemic lupus erythematosus. The exact cause is uncertain; infections, drugs, toxins and pollutants are suspected triggers, and treatment usually involves immunosuppressive drugs.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.3.3 (autoimmune diseases: type-1 diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis); multiple sclerosis is a standard fourth example.

questions.question: What is phagocytosis? Name some WBCs acting as phagocytes.
questions.answer:
Phagocytosis is the process by which a cell engulfs and digests solid particles such as bacteria, dead cells or cell debris. It is a major non-specific defence of the second line.

The phagocyte recognises the microbe by surface receptors that bind microbial molecules such as peptidoglycan, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin and lipopeptides. It extends pseudopodia around the particle and encloses it in a vesicle called a phagosome. The phagosome fuses with a lysosome to form a phagolysosome, and hydrolytic enzymes and antimicrobial substances digest the microbe. Fragments may then be displayed on MHC-II as antigen.

The main white blood cells that act as phagocytes are:

1. Neutrophils — the most abundant leukocytes (50–70%); they migrate rapidly to infected tissues and are specially adapted to phagocytose bacteria.
2. Monocytes — circulating cells (2–8% of leukocytes) that enter tissues and mature into macrophages.
3. Macrophages — large, long-lived tissue phagocytes (for example alveolar macrophages, Kupffer cells and microglia).
4. Dendritic cells — phagocytic cells that capture antigen and present it to T cells.

Eosinophils and basophils are also capable of phagocytosis to a limited extent.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.1 (phagocytosis and the killing cells of blood).

questions.question: What is inflammation?
questions.answer:
Inflammation is a localised, non-specific response of the body to injury or infection. It brings plasma proteins, blood cells and antimicrobial substances to the site of damage, isolates the injurious agent, destroys or removes it, and prepares the tissue for repair.

It is triggered by tissue injury, infection, burns, chemicals or allergens. Damaged mast cells and basophils release histamine, and prostaglandins are produced; these cause vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. As a result the area becomes red and warm, fluid and cells accumulate (swelling), and chemical mediators stimulate pain receptors. Chemotactic factors attract neutrophils and monocytes, which phagocytose the pathogen and dead tissue. Pus, consisting of dead neutrophils, bacteria and tissue debris, may collect. The classical signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function.

Inflammation is protective, but if it persists it may become chronic, as in rheumatoid arthritis. It is controlled by removal of the stimulus, by feedback mechanisms and by anti-inflammatory drugs, and the tissue is then repaired.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.3 (inflammation, cardinal signs, histamine and prostaglandins, pus) and the rheumatoid arthritis box.

questions.question: Outline the harmful effects of fever.
questions.answer:
Although fever is a protective defence, a high or prolonged fever is harmful:

1. Energy loss. The body burns extra fuel to maintain a high metabolic rate and to produce heat, causing weakness, tiredness and weight loss.
2. Discomfort and pain. Fever is accompanied by headache, body ache, chills, shivering and malaise.
3. Dehydration. Sweating, vomiting and a raised breathing rate increase fluid loss, and a raised metabolic rate increases the need for water.
4. Increased work for the heart and lungs. Each 1°C rise increases the heart rate and respiratory rate, which is dangerous in patients with heart or lung disease.
5. Febrile seizures. In infants and young children a rapidly rising temperature may cause convulsions.
6. Enzyme and protein damage. Body temperature above about 105°F (40.6°C) can denature enzymes and other proteins, damage brain cells and, if not controlled, cause death.
7. Loss of appetite and dehydration can delay recovery, and prolonged fever may indicate a serious underlying infection.

For these reasons high fever is controlled with antipyretics, fluids and treatment of the underlying cause.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.4 (harmful effects of fever; temperature above 105°F denatures proteins).

questions.question: State and explain how a bacterium is identified as non-self by our immune system.
questions.answer:
The immune system must distinguish the body's own molecules (self) from those of invading microorganisms (non-self). A bacterium is identified as non-self because it carries molecules that are absent from human cells, and these molecules are recognised by several overlapping mechanisms.

1. Antigens and epitopes. Any foreign macromolecule that can elicit an immune response is called an antigen. Proteins and polysaccharides on the bacterial surface, such as cell-wall peptidoglycan, lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria, flagellin and lipoproteins, act as antigens. The immune system recognises small parts of these molecules called epitopes.

2. Innate recognition by phagocytes. Neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells carry surface receptors for conserved microbial molecules (pathogen-associated molecular patterns). The textbook names peptidoglycan, flagellin, lipopolysaccharides and lipopeptides as the bacterial molecules recognised. Binding of these molecules triggers phagocytosis and the release of cytokines and interferons. Because humans do not make these molecules, their presence signals 'non-self'.

3. Complement and opsonisation. Bacterial surfaces activate the complement system, which coats the bacterium with complement proteins (opsonisation), attracts phagocytes and can lyse the bacterial membrane. Antibodies can also coat bacteria and make them easier to engulf.

4. Antigen presentation and adaptive recognition. After phagocytosis, dendritic cells and macrophages digest the bacterium and display bacterial peptide fragments on MHC-II molecules. They carry the peptide–MHC-II complex to the surface and present it to helper T (TH) cells. The TH cell's T-cell receptor binds the foreign peptide–MHC-II combination, and co-stimulatory signals (for example B7–CD28) confirm that the antigen is foreign. The TH cell is activated and releases cytokines.

5. B cells and antibodies. B lymphocytes carry B-cell receptors (membrane antibodies) that bind native bacterial antigens. With TH help, the selected B cell proliferates (clonal selection), differentiates into plasma cells and secretes antibodies specific to the bacterium. Antibodies neutralise, agglutinate or opsonise the bacterium and activate complement.

6. Cytotoxic T cells. When bacteria multiply inside host cells, bacterial peptides are displayed on MHC-I of the infected cell. CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognise this foreign peptide–MHC-I complex and kill the infected cell, depriving the bacterium of its habitat.

7. Self-recognition and missing self. All nucleated body cells display self-peptides on MHC-I. When MHC-I is normal, NK cells are inhibited; when it is lost or altered, as in infected or tumour cells, NK cells treat the cell as non-self and destroy it. Self-reactive lymphocytes are normally eliminated or suppressed, which prevents attack on the body's own tissues.

In this way the immune system uses microbial surface molecules as non-self flags, reinforces the signal by antigen presentation to T cells and by antibody production, and finally destroys the bacterium through phagocytosis, complement, antibodies and cytotoxic cells. Memory B and T cells remain so that a second infection by the same bacterium is dealt with more rapidly.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 13.2.1 (phagocyte receptors for bacterial molecules), 13.2.2 (complement), 13.3 (antigen, self/non-self, MHC-I/II) and 13.3.2 (T and B cells); the presentation and clonal-selection steps are amplified from standard immunology.

questions.question: What is cytotoxicity? Compare and contrast the mechanisms of NK cell and Tc cell.
questions.answer:
Cytotoxicity is the ability of a cell or substance to damage or kill a target cell. In immunity it refers to the killing of virus-infected cells, tumour cells and other abnormal cells by cytotoxic lymphocytes. The two main cytotoxic cells are natural killer (NK) cells and cytotoxic T (Tc) cells. Both arise from the lymphoid lineage in bone marrow, both kill by inducing apoptosis, and both use perforin and granzymes, but they differ in how they recognise a target and in their specificity.

Mechanism of NK cells:
1. NK cells circulate in blood and patrol tissues as part of the innate immune system. They are not MHC-restricted and have no T-cell receptor.
2. They carry inhibitory receptors for MHC-I. If a cell displays normal MHC-I, the inhibitory signal stops the NK cell. If MHC-I is missing or altered — 'missing self', as in virus-infected or tumour cells — the inhibition is lost and the NK cell is activated.
3. Activated NK cells release perforin, which forms pores in the target membrane, and granzymes, which enter through the pores and activate caspases, causing programmed cell death (apoptosis).
4. NK cells also secrete cytokines such as interferon-γ, and can kill antibody-coated cells by antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).
5. They act within hours, without prior exposure to the antigen, and show little immunological memory.

Mechanism of Tc cells:
1. Tc cells are CD8-bearing T lymphocytes of the adaptive immune system. Each Tc cell carries a TCR that is specific for one antigen.
2. They recognise antigen only when the peptide is displayed on MHC-I on the surface of a nucleated target cell (MHC restriction). They are activated when an antigen-presenting cell presents the antigen together with co-stimulatory signals and helper-T-cell cytokines.
3. The activated Tc cell proliferates and differentiates into a clone of effector cells and memory cells.
4. Effector Tc cells bind the target, release perforin and granzymes, and may also trigger apoptosis through Fas ligand. They secrete IFN-γ and TNF-α and then move on to kill another target — hence they are called 'serial killers'.
5. They act after a delay of several days, are highly specific, and leave memory T cells that give a rapid response on re-exposure.

Comparison:
- Specificity: NK non-specific; Tc antigen-specific.
- Recognition: NK detects missing/altered MHC-I; Tc recognises foreign peptide on MHC-I.
- Receptor: NK has no TCR; Tc has a TCR and CD8.
- Activation: NK is ready immediately; Tc needs antigen presentation, co-stimulation and helper-T cytokines.
- Timing: NK acts within hours (innate); Tc takes days (adaptive).
- Memory: NK has little or none; Tc produces memory cells.
- Shared features: both are lymphoid in origin, both kill by perforin/granzyme-induced apoptosis, and both defend against viruses and tumours.

Thus NK cells provide a rapid first-line cytotoxic defence, while Tc cells provide specific, long-lasting and memory-bearing cytotoxicity.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.1 (cytotoxicity: NK cells, MHC-I 'missing self', perforin/granzyme; Tc cells, CD8, 'serial killers', memory T cells), together with the adaptive-immunity section 13.3.2.

questions.question: What is inflammation? Why it is developed and how it is controlled?
questions.answer:
Inflammation is a localised, non-specific response to tissue injury or infection. It is one of the four major responses of the second line of defence. The classical signs are redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumour), pain (dolor) and loss of function (functio laesa).

Why inflammation develops:
Inflammation is protective. It isolates the site of injury, prevents the spread of pathogens, brings phagocytes and antimicrobial proteins to the area, removes dead cells and debris, and creates conditions for tissue repair. Without it, infection could spread rapidly through the body. It develops when tissue is damaged by infection, cuts, burns, chemicals, radiation or an allergic reaction, or when pathogens breach the first line of defence.

Mechanism:
1. Tissue injury or infection stimulates mast cells and basophils to release histamine, and prostaglandins and other mediators are produced at the site.
2. Histamine and prostaglandins cause vasodilation of arterioles, so more blood flows to the area and it becomes red and warm.
3. They increase capillary permeability, so plasma proteins and fluid leak into the tissue, producing swelling and pain. Prostaglandins and bradykinin sensitise pain receptors.
4. Chemotactic factors attract neutrophils and monocytes from the blood. Neutrophils arrive first and phagocytose bacteria; monocytes become macrophages.
5. Phagocytes and antimicrobial proteins destroy the pathogen, dead tissue is removed, and pus — dead neutrophils, bacteria and debris — may collect.
6. Once the stimulus is removed, the response subsides and fibroblasts and endothelial cells repair the tissue.

How it is controlled:
Inflammation is self-limiting in normal circumstances. Removal and destruction of the pathogen eliminates the trigger. Macrophages clear debris and release anti-inflammatory cytokines; suppressor/regulatory T cells and feedback inhibition reduce the response. Anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, antihistamines) inhibit prostaglandins or histamine and relieve the signs. If the cause persists, the response becomes chronic, with continued tissue destruction and scarring; rheumatoid arthritis is an example of chronic autoimmune inflammation of the joints. In such cases immunosuppressive drugs may be needed.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 13.2.3 (inflammation, histamine, prostaglandins, chemotaxis, cardinal signs, pus) and the rheumatoid arthritis box; control mechanisms include standard immunology.

questions.question: Explain the underlying mechanism of the fever. State and explain its protective role as well as harmful effects.
questions.answer:
Fever (pyrexia) is an abnormal rise in body temperature above the normal set point of about 98.6°F (37°C). It is a non-specific defence of the second line of immunity.

Mechanism:
1. Fever is triggered by pyrogens. Exogenous pyrogens include bacterial toxins and endotoxins; endogenous pyrogens include cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-6, tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and interferon-α, released by phagocytes and other cells in response to infection or inflammation.
2. The pyrogens travel in the blood to the hypothalamus, the temperature-regulating centre of the brain.
3. The hypothalamus responds by producing prostaglandin (PGE2), which raises the temperature set point.
4. The body now behaves as if it were too cold: cutaneous blood vessels constrict so less heat is lost, sweating decreases, and shivering and increased metabolism generate more heat. Body temperature rises until it reaches the new set point.
5. When the pyrogens are removed and prostaglandin production falls, the set point returns to normal. The body then loses heat by sweating and vasodilation, and the temperature falls (the 'crisis').

Protective role:
- Many bacteria and fungi cannot grow or multiply at a raised temperature.
- Fever enhances phagocytosis and speeds up the immune response.
- It increases metabolic activity and the movement of white blood cells to the site of infection.
- It is a signal that infection is present and helps in the response to it.

Harmful effects:
- Fever is metabolically expensive and causes fatigue, weakness, headache, body ache and loss of appetite.
- Perspiration and increased breathing cause dehydration.
- Each degree of temperature rise increases the heart and respiratory rates, which strains the heart and lungs.
- In infants and young children, fever may cause febrile seizures.
- Temperature above about 105°F (40.6°C) denatures enzymes and other proteins, damages brain cells and can cause death if not controlled.
- Prolonged fever may itself cause tissue damage and delay recovery.

For these reasons high fever is treated with antipyretics (aspirin, paracetamol, ibuprofen), which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in the hypothalamus and lower the set point, together with fluids and treatment of the underlying infection.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.2.4 (pyrogens, hypothalamus and prostaglandin, protective role, harmful effects above 105°F) and the antipyretic box.

questions.question: Discuss the structural features of antibody? How it is helpful in getting rid of pathogenic organisms.
questions.answer:
An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a soluble protein produced by plasma cells in response to an antigen. It is Y-shaped and has a highly variable antigen-binding region at the tips of the Y and a constant region that carries out effector functions.

Structural features:
1. Four polypeptide chains. Each antibody molecule consists of two identical heavy (H) chains and two identical light (L) chains, held together by disulfide bonds.
2. Variable and constant regions. The amino-terminal part of each chain is the variable region (VH and VL); its amino-acid sequence differs from one antibody to another and forms the antigen-binding site. The rest is the constant region (CH and CL), which is the same within a class and determines how the antibody is handled by the body.
3. Antigen-binding sites. The paired VH and VL domains at the two tips form two identical antigen-binding sites, so a single IgG molecule can bind two epitopes. The shape of the site is complementary to the epitope.
4. Fab and Fc portions. The two 'arms' of the Y are the Fab (antigen-binding fragment) portions. The stem is the Fc (crystallisable) portion, made of the constant regions of the heavy chains; it binds complement and Fc receptors on phagocytes.
5. Hinge region. A flexible hinge between Fab and Fc allows the two arms to move and bind antigens that are spaced apart.
6. B-cell receptor. A B cell carries a membrane-bound form of the antibody as its B-cell receptor (BCR); the same cell, after activation, secretes the soluble form.
7. Classes. Differences in the heavy-chain constant region produce five classes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. IgG is the main circulating antibody and crosses the placenta; IgA is secreted in milk, saliva and mucus; IgM is a pentamer and acts early; IgE binds mast cells in allergy; IgD is mainly a B-cell receptor.

How antibodies help remove pathogens:
- Neutralisation: antibodies cover the surface proteins of viruses and the toxins of bacteria, preventing them from binding to host cells.
- Agglutination: each antibody can link two antigens, so bacteria or viruses clump together and are easier to phagocytose.
- Precipitation: soluble antigens and antibodies form complexes that are removed by phagocytes.
- Opsonisation: the Fc portion of the antibody binds Fc receptors on macrophages and neutrophils, greatly enhancing phagocytosis.
- Complement activation: the Fc portion activates the classical complement pathway, producing pores in the bacterial membrane (membrane attack complex) and promoting inflammation and phagocytosis.
- Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC): NK cells bind antibody-coated target cells through Fc receptors and kill them.
- Toxin neutralisation and immobilisation: antibodies neutralise bacterial toxins (antitoxins) and immobilise motile organisms.

Thus the variable regions give antibodies their specificity, while the constant regions recruit phagocytes, complement and NK cells to destroy the pathogen. Memory B cells ensure a faster and stronger response on re-exposure.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.3.2 and Fig. 13.13 (BCR made of heavy and light chains with variable and constant regions); the detailed Fab/Fc structure, antibody classes and effector functions are standard immunology required by this exercise.

questions.question: What do you understand by autoimmune disorder? Explain the role of T cells and B cells in transplant rejection.
questions.answer:
An autoimmune disorder is a condition in which the immune system fails to recognise the body's own tissues as self and mounts an immune attack against them. Normally, self-reactive lymphocytes are eliminated or kept under control (self-tolerance). If this tolerance breaks down, autoantibodies and cytotoxic T cells destroy the body's own cells. The exact cause is uncertain; genetic predisposition, bacterial or viral infections, drugs, toxins and pollutants are suspected triggers. Commonly affected tissues include muscles, joints, blood vessels and connective tissue, and symptoms include malaise, low fever, fatigue, muscle ache and rashes. Examples are type-1 diabetes mellitus (destruction of pancreatic β-cells), rheumatoid arthritis (inflammation and destruction of joints), psoriasis (skin) and multiple sclerosis (myelin). Treatment aims to reduce the immune attack with immunosuppressive drugs and to replace the missing product, such as insulin.

Transplant rejection:
A transplant (graft) is tissue or an organ — commonly kidney, liver, heart or skin — taken from a donor and placed in a recipient. Because donor and recipient are genetically different, the donor tissue carries foreign MHC (HLA) molecules and is recognised as non-self. Rejection can be cell-mediated or antibody-mediated.

Role of T cells:
1. Donor dendritic cells migrate from the graft to the recipient's lymphoid tissue and present donor antigens to recipient helper T (TH) cells. Recipient APCs can also pick up donor antigens and present them on self MHC-II (indirect presentation).
2. Activated TH cells proliferate and release cytokines such as IL-2 and interferon-γ.
3. These cytokines activate cytotoxic T (Tc) cells, which recognise donor MHC-I on the graft cells and kill them with perforin and granzymes. They also activate NK cells and macrophages, which attack the graft.
4. Memory T cells are formed, so a second transplant from the same donor is rejected more rapidly.

Role of B cells:
1. Activated TH cells stimulate B cells that have bound donor antigens. The B cells differentiate into plasma cells and secrete antibodies against donor MHC and other graft antigens.
2. Antibodies bind the graft endothelium, activate complement and attract neutrophils and macrophages, causing rapid destruction of the graft (humoral or antibody-mediated rejection).
3. Some antibodies may also cause hyperacute rejection in a recipient who already has preformed antibodies.

Because both T and B cells mediate rejection, transplant recipients are given immunosuppressive drugs (for example cyclosporine, tacrolimus, steroids) to inhibit lymphocyte activation and antibody production. Donor–recipient tissue matching (HLA typing) and regular monitoring reduce the risk, but immunosuppression has side effects such as infections, diabetes, hypertension and osteoporosis.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 13.3.3 (autoimmune diseases; transplant rejection mediated by T cells and B cells; immunosuppressant box).

questions.answer: (a) Alveoli

Their walls are only one cell thick and are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries, so oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse across the alveolar membrane. The pharynx, larynx and trachea are conducting passages and do not carry out gas exchange.

questions.question: When breathing process develop in animals?
questions.answer:
Breathing (ventilation) develops in animals when the body becomes too large and too active for oxygen to reach every cell by diffusion through the body surface alone. In small or thin animals, gases can diffuse directly between the environment and the cells. As animals increase in size, their surface-area-to-volume ratio falls and the diffusion distance becomes too great, so specialised respiratory surfaces and a mechanism to move the respiratory medium over them become necessary.

In mammals, the respiratory system develops from the embryonic foregut; the lungs form as outgrowths of the foregut and become functional before birth. Fetal breathing movements begin in the uterus, and regular, continuous breathing starts at birth with the first breath, when the lungs inflate and the alveolar capillaries are perfused.

Evolutionarily, ventilation appeared with gills in aquatic animals and with lungs in air-breathing vertebrates; both ensure a continuous supply of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide to match the metabolic rate of the animal.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.1 (respiration, ventilation and respiratory surfaces); the embryonic and evolutionary context is standard biology.

questions.question: What type of ventilation occur in human?
questions.answer: Humans use negative pressure breathing, also called tidal ventilation. Air is not pushed into the lungs; instead, the volume of the thoracic cavity is increased so that the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air is drawn in. Inspiration is an active process: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs and sternum, increasing the volume of the thorax. Expiration at rest is passive: these muscles relax, the diaphragm returns to its dome shape, the ribs move down and in, the thoracic volume decreases and air is expelled. The lungs are ventilated in both directions through the same conducting airways, and the air moves in and out like a tide, hence the name tidal ventilation.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.1.7 (ventilation, negative pressure breathing, inspiration and expiration).

questions.question: Why rate of breathing increases in human beings?
questions.answer:
The rate of breathing increases whenever the body's demand for oxygen rises and more carbon dioxide is produced. During exercise, the muscles consume oxygen faster and release more CO2, which dissolves in the blood as carbonic acid and releases H+ ions. The rise in CO2 and H+ is detected by chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (in the carotid arteries), aortic bodies (in the aorta) and the medulla oblongata. These receptors send impulses to the respiratory centre in the medulla oblongata and pons, which increases the rate and depth of breathing.

As a result, more fresh air reaches the alveoli, oxygen uptake increases, and the extra CO2 is removed. Breathing also increases after climbing stairs, running or heavy work, and in fever, pain, anxiety and low blood oxygen, because all of these conditions increase metabolic rate or stimulate the respiratory centre.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.1.7.5 (control of breathing: CO2 and H+, carotid and aortic bodies, medulla oblongata).

questions.question: Why breathing of human being called negative pressure breathing?
questions.answer: Human breathing is called negative pressure breathing because air enters the lungs when the pressure inside the lungs is made lower (negative) relative to atmospheric pressure. During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs and sternum. The volume of the thoracic cavity increases, and because the lungs are sealed inside the pleural membranes and follow the movements of the chest wall, they expand as well. According to Boyle's law, the pressure inside the expanding lungs falls below atmospheric pressure. Air therefore flows from the higher atmospheric pressure outside into the lower pressure in the alveoli. During expiration, the muscles relax, the thoracic volume decreases, the intrapulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air is pushed out. Thus the pressure in the lungs is always lower than atmospheric pressure during inspiration, hence 'negative pressure breathing'.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.1.7 (mechanism of ventilation: pressure changes, negative pressure breathing).

questions.question: How CO2 from cell transport to lungs?
questions.answer:
Carbon dioxide is produced in the tissues by cellular respiration. It diffuses from the cells into the blood and is carried to the lungs in three ways:

1. As bicarbonate ions — about 70%. CO2 diffuses into red blood cells, where the enzyme carbonic anhydrase catalyses its reaction with water: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−. The bicarbonate ions leave the red cells and are carried in the plasma, mainly as sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), while H+ is buffered by haemoglobin.
2. As carbaminohaemoglobin — about 20%. CO2 combines with the amino groups of haemoglobin (and other proteins) to form carbaminohaemoglobin: CO2 + Hb ⇌ HbCO2. This occurs more readily when haemoglobin is deoxygenated.
3. Dissolved in plasma — about 10%. A small amount of CO2 simply dissolves in the water of the plasma.

At the lungs, the low CO2 concentration and high oxygen partial pressure in the alveolar air reverse these reactions. Bicarbonate is converted back to CO2, carbaminohaemoglobin releases CO2, and dissolved CO2 diffuses out of the plasma. All of it then diffuses from the blood across the alveolar membrane into the alveoli and is removed during expiration.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.2.2 (transport of CO2: about 70% bicarbonate, 20% carbaminohaemoglobin, 10% dissolved; carbonic anhydrase).

questions.question: Which of the pigment is called respiratory pigment?
questions.answer:
The respiratory pigments are coloured, iron-containing proteins that increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood and tissues. The main ones are haemoglobin and myoglobin.

Haemoglobin is found in the red blood cells of all vertebrates. It is a conjugated protein made of two pairs of polypeptide chains, each chain carrying an iron-containing heme group. One haemoglobin molecule can bind four molecules of oxygen loosely and reversibly to form oxyhaemoglobin (Hb + 4O2 ⇌ Hb(O2)4). It takes up oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues, and it also helps to carry carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

Myoglobin is a smaller, single-chain globular protein found in muscle. It has one heme group and binds one molecule of oxygen more tightly than haemoglobin, so it stores oxygen in muscle and releases it when the muscle needs it during vigorous activity.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.2.3 (respiratory pigments: haemoglobin and myoglobin, iron-bound proteins, haemoglobin carries four O2).

questions.question: Why hair and mucus glands are present in nostrils and trachea?
questions.answer:
Hair and mucus glands in the nostrils and trachea protect the respiratory system by filtering, moistening and warming the incoming air.

1. In the nostrils, coarse hairs trap dust particles, insects and other large particles, while mucus secreted by the nasal lining traps smaller particles and microorganisms. The ciliated cells move the contaminated mucus toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. The moist surface also humidifies the air and the rich blood supply warms it.
2. In the trachea, mucus glands secrete mucus that traps dust and microbes, and the ciliated columnar epithelium beats in a coordinated way to move the mucus upward to the pharynx — the mucociliary escalator. This prevents particles from reaching the alveoli, where they could cause infection or damage.

The hairs and mucus therefore clean, moisten and warm the air, and they form an important part of the first line of defence of the respiratory tract.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 14.1.4 (nose, trachea and ciliated epithelium) and 13.1 (respiratory-tract first line of defence).

questions.question: How exchange of gases occurs at the alveolar level?
questions.answer:
Gaseous exchange at the alveolar level occurs by simple diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane, driven by differences in partial pressure.

1. The alveolar air has a higher partial pressure of oxygen than the deoxygenated blood in the pulmonary capillaries, so oxygen diffuses from the alveoli through the thin, moist alveolar wall and the capillary endothelium into the blood. There it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin.
2. The blood arriving at the lungs has a higher partial pressure of carbon dioxide than the alveolar air, so carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction — from the blood into the alveoli — and is removed during expiration.
3. The alveolar wall is only about one micrometre thick, is moist (so gases dissolve), and is surrounded by a dense capillary network; these features make diffusion rapid and efficient. Ventilation continually replaces alveolar air, and blood flow through the capillaries is matched to it, maintaining the concentration gradients.

Thus oxygen moves from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli, and the blood leaving the lungs is oxygenated.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 14.1.1–14.1.3 (alveoli, respiratory surface characters, diffusion gradient) and 14.2 (exchange by simple diffusion).

questions.question: What is respiration? Describe human respiratory system?
questions.answer:
Respiration is the process by which the cells of an organism gain energy-rich ATP molecules by oxidising food molecules. In humans the chief food molecule is glucose, and aerobic respiration oxidises glucose with oxygen, releasing energy along with carbon dioxide and water:

C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

Respiration therefore includes breathing (ventilation), the exchange of gases in the lungs and tissues, and the cellular oxidation of food. Ventilation is the movement of air from the atmosphere into the lungs and back; gaseous exchange is the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the respiratory surfaces.

The human respiratory system consists of the respiratory tract and the lungs.

1. External nares and nasal cavity. Air enters through the paired nostrils (external nares) into the nasal chambers, which are separated by the nasal septum. Hairs and cilia trap dust, mucus moistens the air, and the rich blood supply warms it, so the nose acts as an air conditioner. The air then passes through the internal nares into the pharynx.
2. Pharynx. The pharynx is a muscular tube about 13 cm long behind the mouth and nose. It is a common passage for air and food and is divided into the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx.
3. Larynx. The larynx (voice box) lies at the entrance of the trachea. It is made of cartilage, contains the vocal cords that produce sound, and is guarded by the epiglottis, which closes during swallowing to prevent food from entering the airway.
4. Trachea. The windpipe is a fibro-cartilaginous tube about 10–11 cm long. Its wall contains 16–20 C-shaped cartilage rings that keep it open, and its ciliated epithelium and mucus glands trap and move particles upward. At its lower end it divides into the right and left primary bronchi; the right bronchus is wider, shorter and straighter.
5. Bronchi and bronchioles. Each primary bronchus enters a lung and divides into secondary bronchi (one for each lobe), tertiary bronchi and progressively smaller bronchioles. These form the bronchial tree.
6. Alveoli. The bronchioles end in alveolar ducts and clusters of alveoli. Each alveolus is a thin-walled, moist air sac surrounded by capillaries; it is here that oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged. The alveoli give the lungs a very large surface area.
7. Lungs. The two lungs are soft, spongy, highly vascular organs in the thoracic cavity. The left lung is smaller because the heart displaces it; the right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) and the left lung has two (superior, inferior).
8. Thorax and pleura. The lungs are protected by 12 pairs of ribs and the sternum, with the intercostal muscles between the ribs. Each lung is covered by a visceral pleura and the chest wall is lined by a parietal pleura; the pleural cavity between them contains serous fluid that lubricates the surfaces and allows the lungs to expand and contract smoothly. The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdomen and is the chief muscle of inspiration.
questions.explanation: Textbook sections 14.1 (respiration), 14.1.2–14.1.3 (respiratory surface and alveoli) and 14.1.4–14.1.5 (human respiratory organs, lungs, thorax and pleura).

questions.question: What are the 5 main functions of the respiratory system?
questions.answer:
The respiratory system performs the following five main functions:

1. Supply of oxygen. It provides a continuous supply of oxygen to all tissues. Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, binds to haemoglobin and is carried by the circulatory system to every cell for aerobic respiration.
2. Removal of carbon dioxide. It removes carbon dioxide, the by-product of cellular respiration, from the body. CO2 diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is expelled during expiration; this also helps to regulate the acid-base balance of the blood.
3. Exchange (conservation) of gases. The respiratory surfaces regulate the exchange of gases between the internal and external environment of the body. Ventilation brings fresh air to the alveoli and removes stale air, maintaining the concentration gradients for diffusion.
4. Humidification and warming of air. The respiratory system acts as a humidifier and air conditioner: the nose and airways add water vapour to the inhaled air and warm it to body temperature, protecting the delicate alveoli.
5. Filtration and defence. Hairs, mucus, cilia and the cough reflex trap and remove dust, microbes and other particles, while lymphoid tissue and alveolar macrophages defend the lungs against infection.

In addition, the respiratory system participates in sound production (larynx), smell (olfactory receptors in the nasal cavity), and the regulation of blood pH through the control of CO2.
questions.explanation: Textbook section 14.1.6.3 (oxygen supplier, withdrawal, exchange of gas, humidifier); filtration/defence is described in the nose and trachea sections, and the additional roles are standard biology.

questions.question: Draw labelled diagram of human respiratory system.
questions.answer:
Diagram (described):

Draw a front view of the head, neck and thorax. In the head, show the nasal cavity opening at the external nares and the mouth below it; both lead back into the pharynx. Continue downward with the larynx (with the epiglottis and vocal cords), then the trachea with its C-shaped cartilage rings. At the base of the neck the trachea divides into the right and left primary bronchi, which enter the two lungs. Inside each lung, show the bronchi dividing into secondary and tertiary bronchi and then into fine bronchioles ending in clusters of alveoli. Draw the right lung with three lobes (superior, middle and inferior) and the left lung with two lobes (superior and inferior), leaving a notch for the heart. Surround each lung with a double line representing the visceral and parietal pleurae.
